news.headline_zh: 人偏肺病毒本期公共卫生新闻动态
news.lead_zh: 本期人偏肺病毒新闻集中呈现以下动态。
key_findings_zh: 台湾开展的一项为期三年的多中心观察性 队列研究 研究追踪了住院儿科患者中 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 的流行病学模式、临床表现和基因组特征。研究发现,在 监测 年间,受影响儿童的年龄分布逐渐向年龄较小的婴儿转变。 [news-ffd4986fa18391a2]
一项计算药物发现研究确定了三种候选小分子抑制剂,它们对 人偏肺病毒 核衣壳蛋白表现出良好的结合亲和力、结构稳定性和药物样特性。该研究由 Bioengineer.org 报道。 [news-8b0691cb60ddd75d]
本文讨论了 人偏肺病毒 (hMPV) 及其与呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 的比较。报告称,2024年底至2025年初,hMPV在中国造成了暴发,世界卫生组织(WHO)表示,该增幅在季节性变化范围内。 [news-20b34f2db3cd7c34]
进行了多方法统计分析,绘制了共循环呼吸道病毒(包括 人偏肺病毒)在三个流行病学季节的相互作用传播情况。该研究确定了主要呼吸道病毒之间一致的、定向的统计关联模式。 [news-1e8c27dcc97fe59b]
一项多中心横断面研究评估了病毒联合检测对呼吸道合胞病毒 (RSV) 下呼吸道感染 婴儿的临床影响和 流行病学,指出联合检测与较长的住院时间相关(N1、N12、N21)。 [news-86549995c6d5d216]

news.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following Human metapneumovirus news developments.
key_findings_en: A three-year multicenter observational cohort study in Taiwan tracked the epidemiological patterns, clinical manifestations, and genomic features of human metapneumovirus (hMPV) among hospitalized pediatric patients. [news-ffd4986fa18391a2]

A computational drug discovery investigation identified three candidate small-molecule inhibitors that demonstrate favorable binding affinity, structural stability, and drug-like properties against the nucleocapsid protein of human metapneumovirus. The study was reported by Bioengineer.org. [news-8b0691cb60ddd75d]

The article discusses human metapneumovirus (hMPV) and its comparison with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). It reports that hMPV caused an outbreak in China from late 2024 to early 2025, and the World Health Organization (WHO) stated that the increase was within the range of seasonal variation. [news-20b34f2db3cd7c34]

A multi-method statistical analysis was conducted to map the interacting spread of co-circulating respiratory viruses, including human metapneumovirus, across three epidemiological seasons. The study identified consistent, directional patterns of statistical association among major respiratory viruses. [news-1e8c27dcc97fe59b]

A multicenter cross-sectional study evaluated the clinical impact and epidemiology of viral co-detection in infants with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) lower respiratory tract infections, noting that co-detection was associated with longer hospital stays (N1, N12, N21). [news-86549995c6d5d216]

papers.title: Epidemiology and Subtype Distribution of Respiratory Syncytial Virus in Children Aged 0-36 Months With Severe Acute Respiratory Infection in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian Border State, 2022-2024.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: RSV is a leading cause of severe acute respiratory infection (SARI) in children. We describe RSV-associated SARI in children up to 36 months, including seasonality, A/B subtyping, and clinical profile, in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian border state. METHODS: This retrospective, surveillance-based descriptive study used SIVEP-Gripe data on RSV-positive SARI cases notified in 2022-2024. A convenience subset of preserved samples with Ct ≤ 27 (313 typed; 13.9% of cases) underwent duplex RT-qPCR typing. Seasonality was assessed with quasi-Poisson regression; clinical features were compared using chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and Wilcoxon tests. RESULTS: Among 9758 SARI cases, 2254 (23%) were RSV positive. Peak activity was highest in 2023 (Week 14). Most cases (75%) occurred in infants younger than 12 months. Among cases with information, 79.5% (1502/1889) received ventilatory support (8.4% invasive), 14.2% (294/2076) required ICU admission, and 37 died (case fatality 1.6%). From July 2023, with all samples tested for rhinovirus, adenovirus, and human metapneumovirus, 18.4% of cases had codetection, mostly rhinovirus. Among typed samples, RSV-B accounted for 31/37 in 2022 and 104/137 in 2024, and RSV-A accounted for 131/138 in 2023. Deaths among typed cases (6/170 RSV-A and 0/142 RSV-B) all occurred in 2023. CONCLUSIONS: RSV was a frequent cause of SARI hospitalization in this Brazilian border state, mainly among infants. RSV-A and RSV-B cocirculated with comparable clinical profiles; subtype-specific mortality could not be assessed because all deaths among typed cases occurred in 2023. Typed samples were a non-random subset, and clinical data had missing values.

papers.title: Pathogens associated with childhood febrile illness in West Africa: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Background Up to 80% of children seeking medical attention in Africa present with acute febrile illness. Epidemiological data on the locally circulating pathogens causing fever are essential to inform clinical management and for public health interventions. This systematic review sought to understand the aetiologies of febrile illness among children in West Africa. Methods We included healthcare facility and community-based studies with cross-sectional, case-control, and retrospective cross-sectional design which used laboratory methods to detect pathogens causing fever in children aged 1 month to 15 years. A literature search was conducted in Medline and Embase via OVID, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Connecting Repositories (CoRE), Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), African Journals Online (AJOL) and World Health Organisation (WHO) Africa Index Medicus, for studies published from 2013 to 2023. Data was extracted on pathogens detected from routine clinical investigations and study-specific laboratory testing. A risk of bias assessment was conducted using a consolidated CASP checklist developed from the case-control and cross-sectional study checklists. Results We included 84 studies from 11 West African countries. 42% of studies investigated bacterial pathogens in blood, 24% in respiratory samples and 19% in urine, stool, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and ear swabs combined, resulting in the detection of 25 different bacterial species. The most common of these were Salmonella enterica, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Escherichia coli. Seventeen different viruses were detected. Dengue virus, chikungunya virus and West Nile virus were mostly detected from serological studies. Influenza viruses, rhinoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza viruses, human metapneumovirus, coronaviruses, adenoviruses, and enteroviruses were commonly isolated from respiratory samples. Plasmodium falciparum was the most abundant parasite of the 5 different parasites/fungal species detected. Only 8% of studies performed comprehensive investigations (concurrent testing across ≥ 3 pathogen classes in the same participant) for a wide range of pathogens. Conclusion This study found that diagnostic testing was predominantly blood-based, with limited investigation of gastrointestinal, zoonotic, and emerging pathogens. These findings reveal important gaps in the existing evidence base for febrile pathogen detection and highlight areas where future primary research with a broader diagnostic scope would provide more complete epidemiological data. This systematic review has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number: CRD 42023466517. Clinical trials registration Not applicable

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review aimed to understand the aetiologies of febrile illness among children in West Africa. It included 84 studies from 11 countries, highlighting that diagnostic testing was predominantly blood-based, with limited investigation of gastrointestinal, zoonotic, and emerging pathogens. Human metapneumovirus was identified as a significant pathogen, with findings indicating the need for broader diagnostic approaches. The study underscores the importance of comprehensive pathogen detection for improved clinical management and public health interventions. However, the limited number of studies that tested across multiple pathogen classes suggests a gap in the current evidence base. The evidence strength is moderate due to the variability in diagnostic methods and the focus on blood-based testing.

papers.title_zh: 西非儿童发热性疾病相关病原体:系统评价
papers.source_body_en: Background Up to 80% of children seeking medical attention in Africa present with acute febrile illness. Epidemiological data on the locally circulating pathogens causing fever are essential to inform clinical management and for public health interventions. This systematic review sought to understand the aetiologies of febrile illness among children in West Africa. Methods We included healthcare facility and community-based studies with cross-sectional, case-control, and retrospective cross-sectional design which used laboratory methods to detect pathogens causing fever in children aged 1 month to 15 years. A literature search was conducted in Medline and Embase via OVID, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Connecting Repositories (CoRE), Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), African Journals Online (AJOL) and World Health Organisation (WHO) Africa Index Medicus, for studies published from 2013 to 2023. Data was extracted on pathogens detected from routine clinical investigations and study-specific laboratory testing. A risk of bias assessment was conducted using a consolidated CASP checklist developed from the case-control and cross-sectional study checklists. Results We included 84 studies from 11 West African countries. 42% of studies investigated bacterial pathogens in blood, 24% in respiratory samples and 19% in urine, stool, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and ear swabs combined, resulting in the detection of 25 different bacterial species. The most common of these were Salmonella enterica, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, and Escherichia coli. Seventeen different viruses were detected. Dengue virus, chikungunya virus and West Nile virus were mostly detected from serological studies. Influenza viruses, rhinoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza viruses, human metapneumovirus, coronaviruses, adenoviruses, and enteroviruses were commonly isolated from respiratory samples. Plasmodium falciparum was the most abundant parasite of the 5 different parasites/fungal species detected. Only 8% of studies performed comprehensive investigations (concurrent testing across ≥ 3 pathogen classes in the same participant) for a wide range of pathogens. Conclusion This study found that diagnostic testing was predominantly blood-based, with limited investigation of gastrointestinal, zoonotic, and emerging pathogens. These findings reveal important gaps in the existing evidence base for febrile pathogen detection and highlight areas where future primary research with a broader diagnostic scope would provide more complete epidemiological data. This systematic review has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under the registration number: CRD 42023466517. Clinical trials registration Not applicable
papers.abstract_zh: 背景 在非洲就医的儿童中,高达 80% 患有急性发热性疾病。有关当地传播的发烧病原体的流行病学数据对于临床管理和公共卫生干预至关重要。这项系统评价旨在了解西非儿童发热性疾病的病因。方法 我们纳入了医疗机构和社区研究,采用横断面、病例对照和回顾性横断面设计,使用实验室方法检测引起 1 个月至 15 岁儿童发烧的病原体。通过 OVID、Scopus、ScienceDirect、Connecting Repositories (CoRE)、Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ)、African Journals Online (AJOL) 和世界卫生组织 (WHO) Africa Index Medicus 在 Medline 和 Embase 上进行了文献检索,检索 2013 年至 2023 年发表的研究。数据是从常规临床调查和特定研究实验室测试中检测到的病原体中提取的。使用根据病例对照和横断面研究清单开发的综合 CASP 清单进行偏倚风险评估。结果 我们纳入了来自 11 个西非国家的 84 项研究。42% 的研究调查了血液中的细菌病原体,24% 的研究调查了呼吸道样本中的细菌病原体,19% 的研究调查了尿液、粪便、脑脊液 (CSF) 和耳拭子中的细菌病原体,最终检测到了 25 种不同的细菌。其中最常见的是肠道沙门氏菌、肺炎链球菌、金黄色葡萄球菌、流感嗜血杆菌和大肠杆菌。检测到十七种不同的病毒。登革热病毒、基孔肯雅病毒和西尼罗河病毒主要是通过血清学研究检测到的。通常从呼吸道样本中分离出流感病毒、鼻病毒、呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)、副流感病毒、人偏肺病毒、冠状病毒、腺病毒和肠道病毒。恶性疟原虫是检测到的 5 种不同寄生虫/真菌物种中最丰富的寄生虫。只有 8% 的研究对多种病原体进行了全面调查(同一参与者同时测试 ≥ 3 种病原体类别)。结论 这项研究发现诊断检测主要以血液为基础,对胃肠道、人畜共患和新出现的病原体的研究有限。这些发现揭示了发热病原体检测的现有证据基础中的重要差距,并强调了未来具有更广泛诊断范围的初级研究将提供更完整的流行病学数据的领域。该系统评价已在国际前瞻性系统评价注册库(PROSPERO)中注册,注册号:CRD 42023466517。临床试验注册 不适用

papers.title: Generative AI-Driven Hybrid Optimized Deep Learning Model for Computational Intelligence Predicting HMPV Virus Infections in Healthcare
papers.abstract: Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a major etiology of acute respiratory illness, especially among high-risk groups like young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients. Despite its prevalence, HMPV diagnosis is not always accurate due to nonspecific clinical presentation and lack of routine testing, with many cases going undetected or being detected late. Accurate and timely prediction of HMPV infection is important for improving patient outcomes and optimizing healthcare interventions. This paper introduces an innovative AI-based hybrid deep learning framework that integrates Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), CNN-RNN architectures, and Quantum-Inspired Support Vector Machines (QSVM) for precise HMPV prediction. Our approach resolves fundamental problems in medical AI, such as data insufficiency, class imbalance, interpretability, and real-time processing, by introducing three innovations: (1) GAN-based synthetic data augmentation for realistic patient record generation without destroying clinical relationships, substantially boosting the diversity and robustness of training data; (2) a hybrid CNN-RNN model for spatiotemporal feature extraction from multimodal clinical data sources such as Electronic Health Records (EHRs), time-series vitals, and chest X-rays to enable end-to-end pattern recognition and sequence analysis; and (3) QSVM optimization for improved classification in high-dimensional spaces by exploiting quantum-inspired decision boundaries to realize superior separability and minimize misclassification rates. The suggested model has 96.2% accuracy, 96.1% F1-score, and 0.983 AUC-ROC, 5%–7% higher than traditional approaches and 32% fewer false negatives, hence minimizing the chance of undetected instances. To ensure model robustness and generalizability, rigorous cross-validation was conducted across various hospital networks and patient populations. Clinical three-hospital network validation attests to the strength and scalability of the model, with real-time inference times (<200ms) enabling smooth integration into EHR systems and rapid clinical decision support. Further, attention mechanisms integrated into the CNN-RNN model enhance interpretability by highlighting essential features that influence predictions, 59 thereby closing the loop between AI-derived insights and medical reasoning and increasing clinician confidence. The integration of generative augmentation, hybrid modeling, and quantum-inspired optimization makes our framework a state-of-the-art solution for predictive healthcare, significantly improving the early detection and treatment of HMPV infections.

papers.title_zh: 用于预测医疗保健中 HMPV 病毒感染的计算智能的生成式 AI 驱动混合优化深度学习模型
papers.source_body_en: Human Metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a major etiology of acute respiratory illness, especially among high-risk groups like young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised patients. Despite its prevalence, HMPV diagnosis is not always accurate due to nonspecific clinical presentation and lack of routine testing, with many cases going undetected or being detected late. Accurate and timely prediction of HMPV infection is important for improving patient outcomes and optimizing healthcare interventions. This paper introduces an innovative AI-based hybrid deep learning framework that integrates Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), CNN-RNN architectures, and Quantum-Inspired Support Vector Machines (QSVM) for precise HMPV prediction. Our approach resolves fundamental problems in medical AI, such as data insufficiency, class imbalance, interpretability, and real-time processing, by introducing three innovations: (1) GAN-based synthetic data augmentation for realistic patient record generation without destroying clinical relationships, substantially boosting the diversity and robustness of training data; (2) a hybrid CNN-RNN model for spatiotemporal feature extraction from multimodal clinical data sources such as Electronic Health Records (EHRs), time-series vitals, and chest X-rays to enable end-to-end pattern recognition and sequence analysis; and (3) QSVM optimization for improved classification in high-dimensional spaces by exploiting quantum-inspired decision boundaries to realize superior separability and minimize misclassification rates. The suggested model has 96.2% accuracy, 96.1% F1-score, and 0.983 AUC-ROC, 5%–7% higher than traditional approaches and 32% fewer false negatives, hence minimizing the chance of undetected instances. To ensure model robustness and generalizability, rigorous cross-validation was conducted across various hospital networks and patient populations. Clinical three-hospital network validation attests to the strength and scalability of the model, with real-time inference times (<200ms) enabling smooth integration into EHR systems and rapid clinical decision support. Further, attention mechanisms integrated into the CNN-RNN model enhance interpretability by highlighting essential features that influence predictions, 59 thereby closing the loop between AI-derived insights and medical reasoning and increasing clinician confidence. The integration of generative augmentation, hybrid modeling, and quantum-inspired optimization makes our framework a state-of-the-art solution for predictive healthcare, significantly improving the early detection and treatment of HMPV infections.
papers.abstract_zh: 人偏肺病毒 (HMPV) 是急性呼吸道疾病的主要病因,尤其是幼儿、老年人和免疫功能低下患者等高危人群。尽管其为 患病率,但由于非特异性临床表现和缺乏常规检测,HMPV 诊断 并不总是准确的,许多病例未被发现或发现较晚。准确及时地预测 HMPV 感染对于改善患者治疗结果和优化医疗保健干预措施非常重要。本文介绍了一种基于人工智能的创新混合深度学习框架,该框架集成了生成对抗网络 (GAN)、CNN-RNN 架构和量子启发支持 媒介 机器 (QSVM),以实现精确的 HMPV 预测。我们的方法通过引入三项创新,解决了医疗人工智能中的基本问题,例如数据不足、类别不平衡、可解释性和实时处理:(1)基于 GAN 的合成数据增强,可在不破坏临床关系的情况下生成真实的患者记录,从而大大提高训练数据的多样性和鲁棒性;(2) 混合 CNN-RNN 模型,用于从电子健康记录 (EHR)、时间序列生命体征和胸部 X 射线等多模式临床数据源中提取时空特征,以实现端到端模式识别和序列分析;(3) QSVM 优化,通过利用量子启发的决策边界来改进高维空间中的分类,以实现卓越的可分离性并最大限度地减少误分类率。建议的模型具有 96.2% 的准确率、96.1% F1 分数和 0.983 AUC-ROC,比传统方法高 5%–7%,漏报率减少 32%,从而最大限度地减少未检测到实例的机会。为了确保模型的稳健性和普遍性,在不同的医院网络和患者群体中进行了严格的交叉验证。临床三医院网络验证证明了该模型的强度和可扩展性,实时推理时间(<200ms)能够顺利集成到 EHR 系统中并提供快速的临床决策支持。此外,集成到 CNN-RNN 模型中的注意力机制通过突出影响预测的基本特征来增强可解释性,59 从而闭合人工智能得出的见解和医学推理之间的循环,并提高临床医生的信心。生成增强、混合建模和量子优化的集成使我们的框架成为预测医疗保健的最先进的解决方案,显着改善了 HMPV 感染的早期检测和 Z​​XQTERMUQXZ。

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hospitalized Pediatric Human Metapneumovirus Infections Shifted Toward Younger Infants in Taiwan by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Hospitalized Pediatric Human Metapneumovirus Infections Shifted Toward Younger Infants in Taiwan Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A three-year multicenter observational cohort investigation conducted across three hospitals in Taiwan has tracked the epidemiological patterns, clinical manifestations, and genomic features of human metapneumovirus among hospitalized pediatric patients following post-pandemic viral resurgence. Between January 2023 and December 2025, investigators systematically evaluated acute respiratory tract infections in children under eighteen years of age, identifying human metapneumovirus in nearly twelve percent of systematically screened hospital admissions. The research uncovered a notable temporal transition in the age distribution of affected children, marked by a progressive shift from older children toward younger infants over the consecutive surveillance years. The study also characterized co-circulating viral lineages, identified distinct amino acid substitutions within the viral fusion protein in emerging strains, and detailed clinical outcomes across varying levels of hospital care, providing comprehensive epidemiological evidence on pediatric human metapneumovirus activity during the post-pandemic recovery era. Human metapneumovirus was initially identified in 2001 as a widespread respiratory pathogen belonging to the Pneumoviridae family, sharing genetic relationships with respiratory syncytial virus. Worldwide pooled prevalence estimates indicate that the virus accounts for approximately 5.3 percent of respiratory tract infections across all age brackets, reaching its highest documented prevalence of 6.7 percent among children younger than five years and falling to 2.5 percent among adults. The viral genome spans roughly 13,300 base pairs encoding eight genes, with the fusion protein serving as the primary neutralizing antibody target and both the fusion and attachment glycoprotein genes utilized for molecular classification. The pathogen divides into two major genotypes, designated A and B, comprising four circulating sublineages termed A1, A2, B1, and B2. Following extensive disruptions to typical viral seasonality during the COVID-19 pandemic, widespread post-pandemic resurgences were recorded internationally, yet comprehensive clinical and molecular data within Taiwanese healthcare settings remained sparse. To evaluate these dynamics, researchers implemented a hybrid retrospective and prospective cohort protocol collaborating between the National Taiwan University Children’s Hospital, an academic tertiary medical center situated in northern Taiwan, and the Show Chwan Healthcare System, encompassing two community hospitals located in Changhua County within central Taiwan. The investigation enrolled hospitalized children younger than eighteen years diagnosed with acute respiratory illness who underwent molecular testing with either the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2.1 or the Pneumonia Panel. Period 1 spanned January 2023 through June 2024 as a retrospective electronic medical record review, while Period 2 operated prospectively from July 2024 through December 2025, gathering nasopharyngeal swabs and structured clinical records after obtaining written informed parental consent. Across the entire cohort, lower respiratory tract illness was classified by attending physicians into bronchitis, bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia, or pneumonia, while dyspnea was documented by observable nasal flaring or intercostal and subcostal retractions. Discover more Engineering Job Board Research Paper Access Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Across the thirty-six months of hospital surveillance, clinical teams performed molecular screening panels on 3310 hospitalized pediatric admissions presenting with acute respiratory conditions, identifying at least one causative respiratory pathogen in 2652 individuals, representing 80.1 percent of all screened tests. Rhinovirus or enterovirus appeared as the most prevalent detected agent at 38.2 percent, followed in frequency by respiratory syncytial virus at 15.2 percent, parainfluenza viruses at 14.8 percent, adenovirus at 14.4 percent, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae at 12.3 percent. Human metapneumovirus ranked as the sixth most frequent pathogen, detected in 390 patients, or 11.8 percent of tested cases, including 233 detections during the retrospective phase and 157 during the prospective phase. Following the exclusion of forty-eight prospective cases lacking parental consent, the research team analyzed detailed medical, laboratory, and therapeutic records for 342 confirmed pediatric inpatients across the participating institutions. The cohort of 342 hospitalized children exhibited a median age of 2.77 years with an interquartile range from 1.30 to 4.64 years, and male patients comprised 51.2 percent of the population. Lower respiratory tract involvement dominated clinical admissions, documented in 93.6 percent of cases, whereas upper respiratory tract diagnoses accounted for only 6.4 percent. Chronic underlying medical conditions were present in 41.5 percent of the overall cohort, though such comorbidities appeared with significantly greater frequency among children treated at the tertiary children’s hospital than in the community hospital system, recording 61.7 percent versus 19.1 percent. The specific pre-existing diagnoses included low birth weight in 15.2 percent, prematurity in 13.7 percent, asthma in 8.8 percent, congenital heart disease in 5.3 percent, chronic neurological disorders in 4.1 percent, genetic or chromosomal disorders in 1.5 percent, active malignancy in 1.2 percent, and diagnosed immunodeficiency in 0.9 percent. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Read Health Guides Clinical presentations were characterized by fever in 98.2 percent of children, lasting for an overall median duration of 4 days, alongside cough in 95.0 percent, audible wheezing in 34.2 percent, shortness of breath or dyspnea in 33.3 percent, and visible chest retractions in 20.8 percent. Laboratory evaluations demonstrated a median white blood cell count of 8.65 thousand cells per microliter and a median neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio of 1.51 across the study sites. Viral co-infections were confirmed in 43.9 percent of the children, with rhinovirus detected in 24.9 percent, parainfluenza in 9.2 percent, and adenovirus in 8.7 percent. Respiratory bacterial cultures were obtained for 179 children, yielding positive pathogenic cultures in 46.4 percent of tested individuals, predominantly Haemophilus influenzae at 14.6 percent and Moraxella catarrhalis at 14.3 percent, while Streptococcus pneumoniae was confirmed in only 4.4 percent. Radiographic abnormalities, defined as pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrates, were noted in 30.8 percent of evaluated chest radiographs. Hospital management entailed a median inpatient duration of 6 days, with 17.1 percent of evaluated patients requiring pediatric intensive care unit admission and staying an intensive care median of 5 days. Prescribed clinical therapies included systemic or inhaled antibiotics in 66.4 percent of children, bronchodilators in 57.9 percent, and systemic corticosteroid treatments in 17.5 percent, without any fatal outcomes recorded in the cohort. Overall, 39.8 percent of inpatients required some form of respiratory support, encompassing supplemental oxygen in 97 children and advanced respiratory support modalities in 39 cases. Advanced modalities comprised high-flow nasal cannula in 27 individuals, bilevel positive airway pressure in 7 patients, and invasive mechanical ventilation in 5 children. Multivariable regression demonstrated that the need for advanced respiratory support was independently associated with pre-existing neurological disorders, with an adjusted odds ratio of 5.76, and pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrations on radiographs, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.44. Epidemiological surveillance identified an annual seasonal recurrence that was remarkably consistent across all three monitored years, marked by an expansion of viral activity commencing in February, a defined peak in April, and declining detection by July. Simultaneously, analysis of patient demographics demonstrated a progressive decline in the median age of hospitalized children from 3.45 years in 2023 to 3.06 years in 2024, falling to 2.12 years by 2025. Statistical trend testing confirmed that the proportion of hospitalized infants aged zero to one year increased significantly over the three years, while the proportion of affected children older than five years dropped significantly. The authors noted that older children accounted for an elevated share of hospitalizations during the initial 2023 resurgence wave before hospital admissions reverted toward the customary younger pediatric demographic, aligning with international observations documented in Japan and other jurisdictions following post-pandemic re-emergence. Molecular sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of prospective specimens successfully characterized the fusion gene of 124 human metapneumovirus isolates, identifying genotype A in 85 specimens, representing 68.5 percent, and genotype B in 39 specimens, representing 31.5 percent. Phylogenetic trees constructed using maximum-likelihood methods on 78 complete fusion gene coding sequences demonstrated that all four global sublineages co-circulated in Taiwan, with sublineage A2.2.2 constituting the predominant lineage. Furthermore, circulating genotype B2 viruses isolated during the 2025 season were marked by two specific amino acid substitutions in the fusion protein, designated L36H and K179R, which mirrored emerging variant strains identified in regional outbreaks within mainland China during the corresponding 2024 to 2025 period. Comparative clinical analyses between genotype A and genotype B revealed broadly similar symptomatology, diagnoses, and interventions, although children with genotype B presented with a higher frequency of neurological disorders and higher median leukocyte counts. The study authors highlighted several methodological limitations that contextualize their observational conclusions, including the relatively modest number of successfully sequenced viral amplicons and the exclusive analysis of the fusion gene coding region. Because the viral attachment glycoprotein gene was not sequenced, the researchers could not verify whether the predominant A2.2.2 strains harbored the 111-nucleotide or 180-nucleotide gene duplications described in other international cohorts. Additionally, clinical specimens were unavailable for sequencing from the 2023 to 2024 period, preventing uninterrupted continuous molecular tracking across the complete three-year span. The investigators also emphasized that differences in data collection between the retrospective and prospective study phases, potential selection bias from consent requirements, single-country geographic scope, and lack of comparative pathogen controls warrant cautious interpretation of the observed age shifts, underscoring the necessity for sustained multicenter molecular surveillance to monitor ongoing viral evolution and transmission. Following the exclusion of forty-eight prospective cases lacking parental consent, the research team analyzed detailed medical, laboratory, and therapeutic records for 342 confirmed pediatric inpatients across the participating institutions. The cohort of 342 hospitalized children exhibited a median age of 2.77 years with an interquartile range from 1.30 to 4.64 years, and male patients comprised 51.2 percent of the population. Lower respiratory tract involvement dominated clinical admissions, documented in 93.6 percent of cases, whereas upper respiratory tract diagnoses accounted for only 6.4 percent. Chronic underlying medical conditions were present in 41.5 percent of the overall cohort, though such comorbidities appeared with significantly greater frequency among children treated at the tertiary children’s hospital than in the community hospital system, recording 61.7 percent versus 19.1 percent. The specific pre-existing diagnoses included low birth weight in 15.2 percent, prematurity in 13.7 percent, asthma in 8.8 percent, congenital heart disease in 5.3 percent, chronic neurological disorders in 4.1 percent, genetic or chromosomal disorders in 1.5 percent, active malignancy in 1.2 percent, and diagnosed immunodeficiency in 0.9 percent. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Read Health Guides Clinical presentations were characterized by fever in 98.2 percent of children, lasting for an overall median duration of 4 days, alongside cough in 95.0 percent, audible wheezing in 34.2 percent, shortness of breath or dyspnea in 33.3 percent, and visible chest retractions in 20.8 percent. Laboratory evaluations demonstrated a median white blood cell count of 8.65 thousand cells per microliter and a median neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio of 1.51 across the study sites. Viral co-infections were confirmed in 43.9 percent of the children, with rhinovirus detected in 24.9 percent, parainfluenza in 9.2 percent, and adenovirus in 8.7 percent. Respiratory bacterial cultures were obtained for 179 children, yielding positive pathogenic cultures in 46.4 percent of tested individuals, predominantly Haemophilus influenzae at 14.6 percent and Moraxella catarrhalis at 14.3 percent, while Streptococcus pneumoniae was confirmed in only 4.4 percent. Radiographic abnormalities, defined as pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrates, were noted in 30.8 percent of evaluated chest radiographs. Hospital management entailed a median inpatient duration of 6 days, with 17.1 percent of evaluated patients requiring pediatric intensive care unit admission and staying an intensive care median of 5 days. Prescribed clinical therapies included systemic or inhaled antibiotics in 66.4 percent of children, bronchodilators in 57.9 percent, and systemic corticosteroid treatments in 17.5 percent, without any fatal outcomes recorded in the cohort. Overall, 39.8 percent of inpatients required some form of respiratory support, encompassing supplemental oxygen in 97 children and advanced respiratory support modalities in 39 cases. Advanced modalities comprised high-flow nasal cannula in 27 individuals, bilevel positive airway pressure in 7 patients, and invasive mechanical ventilation in 5 children. Multivariable regression demonstrated that the need for advanced respiratory support was independently associated with pre-existing neurological disorders, with an adjusted odds ratio of 5.76, and pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrations on radiographs, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.44. Epidemiological surveillance identified an annual seasonal recurrence that was remarkably consistent across all three monitored years, marked by an expansion of viral activity commencing in February, a defined peak in April, and declining detection by July. Simultaneously, analysis of patient demographics demonstrated a progressive decline in the median age of hospitalized children from 3.45 years in 2023 to 3.06 years in 2024, falling to 2.12 years by 2025. Statistical trend testing confirmed that the proportion of hospitalized infants aged zero to one year increased significantly over the three years, while the proportion of affected children older than five years dropped significantly. The authors noted that older children accounted for an elevated share of hospitalizations during the initial 2023 resurgence wave before hospital admissions reverted toward the customary younger pediatric demographic, aligning with international observations documented in Japan and other jurisdictions following post-pandemic re-emergence. Molecular sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of prospective specimens successfully characterized the fusion gene of 124 human metapneumovirus isolates, identifying genotype A in 85 specimens, representing 68.5 percent, and genotype B in 39 specimens, representing 31.5 percent. Phylogenetic trees constructed using maximum-likelihood methods on 78 complete fusion gene coding sequences demonstrated that all four global sublineages co-circulated in Taiwan, with sublineage A2.2.2 constituting the predominant lineage. Furthermore, circulating genotype B2 viruses isolated during the 2025 season were marked by two specific amino acid substitutions in the fusion protein, designated L36H and K179R, which mirrored emerging variant strains identified in regional outbreaks within mainland China during the corresponding 2024 to 2025 period. Comparative clinical analyses between genotype A and genotype B revealed broadly similar symptomatology, diagnoses, and interventions, although children with genotype B presented with a higher frequency of neurological disorders and higher median leukocyte counts. The study authors highlighted several methodological limitations that contextualize their observational conclusions, including the relatively modest number of successfully sequenced viral amplicons and the exclusive analysis of the fusion gene coding region. Because the viral attachment glycoprotein gene was not sequenced, the researchers could not verify whether the predominant A2.2.2 strains harbored the 111-nucleotide or 180-nucleotide gene duplications described in other international cohorts. Additionally, clinical specimens were unavailable for sequencing from the 2023 to 2024 period, preventing uninterrupted continuous molecular tracking across the complete three-year span. The investigators also emphasized that differences in data collection between the retrospective and prospective study phases, potential selection bias from consent requirements, single-country geographic scope, and lack of comparative pathogen controls warrant cautious interpretation of the observed age shifts, underscoring the necessity for sustained multicenter molecular surveillance to monitor ongoing viral evolution and transmission. news.content: メインコンテンツへスキップ Translated by AI·Show original Photo bygolchiki What is Human Metapneumovirus? How is it different from RSV? こなん Nov 24, 2026 08:55 Many parents may have heard the name "human metapneumovirus (hMPV)" for the first time this winter. From late 2024 to early 2025, reports of an outbreak of this virus in China made headlines. While the World Health Organization (WHO) has explained that this is "within the range of seasonal variation" [3], here is a summary of what research tells us about how it differs from RSV and how concerned parents should be for their children. Here are the three main points Human metapneumovirus is a very common virus that causes colds, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia in children. Almost all children are infected at least once by the time they turn five. Symptoms are identical to those of RSV and influenza, and it is impossible to distinguish them by appearance alone. It spreads from late winter to spring, and hospitalizations are most frequent in children under one year old, especially those between 6 and 12 months of age. There are currently no specific cures or vaccines. Treatment focuses on supportive care, such as hydration and respiratory support, and prevention relies on basic measures like handwashing. Background: A "relative" of RSV discovered in 2001 Human metapneumovirus was discovered in the Netherlands in 2001 and belongs to the same Pneumoviridae family as RSV [3]. Although its discovery is recent, it has actually been circulating among humans for a long time, and it is estimated that 90–100% of children are infected by the age of 5 to 10 [3]. Immunity does not last long even after infection, and people continue to be infected repeatedly into adulthood. The peak of the outbreak in the Northern Hemisphere is from late winter to spring (January to March), which overlaps with the RSV season [3]. It spreads through droplets and contact, moving from the nose and throat to the bronchi and lungs. Symptoms are no different from a common cold, including fever, cough, runny nose, and sore throat, but in infants and young children, it can cause bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and wheezing [3]. Evidence: 14 million cases of lower respiratory tract infections annually in children under 5 Globally, there were an estimated 14.2 million cases in children under 5 in 2018 [1]. A 2021 estimate in The Lancet Global Health (a review and model analysis of 119 studies and 40 unpublished datasets) found that in 2018, there were an estimated 14.2 million cases of human metapneumovirus-associated lower respiratory tract infections in children under 5 worldwide, with 643,000 hospitalizations and 16,100 deaths. 58% of hospitalized children were under 1 year old, indicating that the risk of severe illness is particularly high for those under 12 months. However, most of the deaths were concentrated in low- and middle-income countries, and deaths are extremely rare in medical systems like Japan's. Among patients with respiratory infections, 5.3% tested positive [2]. A 2025 meta-analysis in eClinicalMedicine (611 studies, approximately 2.23 million people) found that the proportion of patients who tested positive for human metapneumovirus among those seeking medical attention for respiratory infections was 5.3% overall, and 6.7% in children under 5. The rate was higher at 8.2% for lower respiratory tract infections and 7.0% for bronchiolitis, while it was 5.5% for pneumonia. In case-control analyses comparing them to asymptomatic individuals, the odds ratio for association with respiratory infection was 4.6, confirming that it is not just a "virus found by chance" but a cause of illness. Evidence: How often does it become severe? Among those who tested positive, about half required hospitalization, and 12% were admitted to the intensive care unit [4]. A 2026 meta-analysis in Open Forum Infectious Diseases (94 studies, approximately 26,000 people) found that among those confirmed positive by testing, 48% required hospitalization, 12% were admitted to the intensive care unit, 8% used a ventilator, and 3% died in the hospital. However, many of the studies included in this analysis focused on hospitalized patients, and those with mild symptoms who did not seek medical attention were mostly excluded. This cannot be read as the severity rate for all infected individuals, and it is appropriate to take it as an indicator that "a certain number of people do become severely ill." The peak for hospitalization is 6 to 12 months of age, which is later than the 2 to 3 months for RSV [3]. Home care and when to see a doctor Because there is no specific cure, home care focuses on the same symptomatic treatments as for a cold: hydration, rest, nasal suction, and humidification. Use age-appropriate fever reducers according to the instructions. Antibiotics do not work on viruses. A drug called ribavirin suppresses the virus in a test tube, but its effectiveness in humans has not been demonstrated [3]. Vaccines have not yet been put into practical use and are currently under development [3]. In outpatient settings, testing for human metapneumovirus is usually not performed because the results would not change the treatment. If the condition is severe enough to require hospitalization, PCR testing may be performed in conjunction with other respiratory viruses [3]. You should see a doctor in the following situations: • Breathing is rapid, the area between the ribs sinks in when inhaling, or the child sounds wheezy and distressed • Unable to drink fluids, lethargic, or lips/face are pale or blue • Fever persists for 3–4 days or longer, or a cough is prolonged and prevents sleep at night • Symptoms are severe in children with a history of premature birth, asthma, or underlying medical conditions Prevention involves basic measures such as handwashing, cough etiquette, and avoiding contact with people who are unwell. Please consult your family doctor for individual advice. Common misconceptions “It’s scary because it’s a new virus” — Although it was discovered in 2001, it is a common virus that has been circulating for a long time. The WHO also considers the increase in China at the end of 2024 to be within the range of seasonal variation [3]. “If I know the name of the virus through testing, the treatment will change” — In outpatient care, even if the virus name is known, the treatment remains symptomatic and does not change. Not testing is not an "oversight," but because it is not necessary for treatment. “Taking antibiotics will make it heal faster” — Antibiotics are drugs that work on bacteria and do not work on viruses. They are not used unless a bacterial complication is suspected. “It’s the same as RSV, so the same measures are fine” — While the timing of outbreaks and symptoms are similar, there are differences, such as the later peak age for hospitalization. In any case, infants under 1 year old are prone to severe illness, so it is important to keep a close eye on their breathing. Summary Human metapneumovirus is a common respiratory virus that circulates from winter to spring, and almost all children are infected by the age of five. Most cases resolve as a cold, but in infants and young children, it can lead to bronchiolitis or pneumonia, with an estimated 640,000+ hospitalizations worldwide annually. news.content_original: メインコンテンツへスキップ Translated by AI·Show original Photo bygolchiki What is Human Metapneumovirus? How is it different from RSV? こなん Nov 24, 2026 08:55 Many parents may have heard the name "human metapneumovirus (hMPV)" for the first time this winter. From late 2024 to early 2025, reports of an outbreak of this virus in China made headlines. While the World Health Organization (WHO) has explained that this is "within the range of seasonal variation" [3], here is a summary of what research tells us about how it differs from RSV and how concerned parents should be for their children. Here are the three main points Human metapneumovirus is a very common virus that causes colds, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia in children. Almost all children are infected at least once by the time they turn five. Symptoms are identical to those of RSV and influenza, and it is impossible to distinguish them by appearance alone. It spreads from late winter to spring, and hospitalizations are most frequent in children under one year old, especially those between 6 and 12 months of age. There are currently no specific cures or vaccines. Treatment focuses on supportive care, such as hydration and respiratory support, and prevention relies on basic measures like handwashing. Background: A "relative" of RSV discovered in 2001 Human metapneumovirus was discovered in the Netherlands in 2001 and belongs to the same Pneumoviridae family as RSV [3]. Although its discovery is recent, it has actually been circulating among humans for a long time, and it is estimated that 90–100% of children are infected by the age of 5 to 10 [3]. Immunity does not last long even after infection, and people continue to be infected repeatedly into adulthood. The peak of the outbreak in the Northern Hemisphere is from late winter to spring (January to March), which overlaps with the RSV season [3]. It spreads through droplets and contact, moving from the nose and throat to the bronchi and lungs. Symptoms are no different from a common cold, including fever, cough, runny nose, and sore throat, but in infants and young children, it can cause bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and wheezing [3]. Evidence: 14 million cases of lower respiratory tract infections annually in children under 5 Globally, there were an estimated 14.2 million cases in children under 5 in 2018 [1]. A 2021 estimate in The Lancet Global Health (a review and model analysis of 119 studies and 40 unpublished datasets) found that in 2018, there were an estimated 14.2 million cases of human metapneumovirus-associated lower respiratory tract infections in children under 5 worldwide, with 643,000 hospitalizations and 16,100 deaths. 58% of hospitalized children were under 1 year old, indicating that the risk of severe illness is particularly high for those under 12 months. However, most of the deaths were concentrated in low- and middle-income countries, and deaths are extremely rare in medical systems like Japan's. Among patients with respiratory infections, 5.3% tested positive [2]. A 2025 meta-analysis in eClinicalMedicine (611 studies, approximately 2.23 million people) found that the proportion of patients who tested positive for human metapneumovirus among those seeking medical attention for respiratory infections was 5.3% overall, and 6.7% in children under 5. The rate was higher at 8.2% for lower respiratory tract infections and 7.0% for bronchiolitis, while it was 5.5% for pneumonia. In case-control analyses comparing them to asymptomatic individuals, the odds ratio for association with respiratory infection was 4.6, confirming that it is not just a "virus found by chance" but a cause of illness. Evidence: How often does it become severe? Among those who tested positive, about half required hospitalization, and 12% were admitted to the intensive care unit [4]. A 2026 meta-analysis in Open Forum Infectious Diseases (94 studies, approximately 26,000 people) found that among those confirmed positive by testing, 48% required hospitalization, 12% were admitted to the intensive care unit, 8% used a ventilator, and 3% died in the hospital. However, many of the studies included in this analysis focused on hospitalized patients, and those with mild symptoms who did not seek medical attention were mostly excluded. This cannot be read as the severity rate for all infected individuals, and it is appropriate to take it as an indicator that "a certain number of people do become severely ill." The peak for hospitalization is 6 to 12 months of age, which is later than the 2 to 3 months for RSV [3]. Home care and when to see a doctor Because there is no specific cure, home care focuses on the same symptomatic treatments as for a cold: hydration, rest, nasal suction, and humidification. Use age-appropriate fever reducers according to the instructions. Antibiotics do not work on viruses. A drug called ribavirin suppresses the virus in a test tube, but its effectiveness in humans has not been demonstrated [3]. Vaccines have not yet been put into practical use and are currently under development [3]. In outpatient settings, testing for human metapneumovirus is usually not performed because the results would not change the treatment. If the condition is severe enough to require hospitalization, PCR testing may be performed in conjunction with other respiratory viruses [3]. You should see a doctor in the following situations: • Breathing is rapid, the area between the ribs sinks in when inhaling, or the child sounds wheezy and distressed • Unable to drink fluids, lethargic, or lips/face are pale or blue • Fever persists for 3–4 days or longer, or a cough is prolonged and prevents sleep at night • Symptoms are severe in children with a history of premature birth, asthma, or underlying medical conditions Prevention involves basic measures such as handwashing, cough etiquette, and avoiding contact with people who are unwell. Please consult your family doctor for individual advice. Common misconceptions “It’s scary because it’s a new virus” — Although it was discovered in 2001, it is a common virus that has been circulating for a long time. The WHO also considers the increase in China at the end of 2024 to be within the range of seasonal variation [3]. “If I know the name of the virus through testing, the treatment will change” — In outpatient care, even if the virus name is known, the treatment remains symptomatic and does not change. Not testing is not an "oversight," but because it is not necessary for treatment. “Taking antibiotics will make it heal faster” — Antibiotics are drugs that work on bacteria and do not work on viruses. They are not used unless a bacterial complication is suspected. “It’s the same as RSV, so the same measures are fine” — While the timing of outbreaks and symptoms are similar, there are differences, such as the later peak age for hospitalization. In any case, infants under 1 year old are prone to severe illness, so it is important to keep a close eye on their breathing. Summary Human metapneumovirus is a common respiratory virus that circulates from winter to spring, and almost all children are infected by the age of five. Most cases resolve as a cold, but in infants and young children, it can lead to bronchiolitis or pneumonia, with an estimated 640,000+ hospitalizations worldwide annually. There is still no specific cure or vaccine, so monitor the child at home with fluids and rest, and see a doctor promptly if breathing seems difficult or if the child cannot take in fluids. "The name is new, but it is actually a virus that has been around for a long time"—knowing this will help you avoid being swayed by the news. References [1] Wang X, et al. Human metapneumovirus, first isolated in 2001 within the family Paramyxoviridae, represents a leading cause of acute respiratory tract infections across all demographics, frequently resulting in severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia requiring hospitalization among pediatric, elderly, and immunocompromised populations. While seasonal outbreaks circulate globally and seroprevalence surveys indicate widespread infection by age five, host immunity remains incomplete, permitting lifelong reinfections transmitted via direct contact, respiratory droplets, and contaminated fomites. Despite this sustained morbidity and documented mortality risks during viral coinfection, there are currently no approved antiviral therapies or protective vaccines directed against the pathogen. Broad-spectrum antiviral treatments such as ribavirin have offered limited clinical efficacy, while monoclonal antibodies directed against the surface fusion protein encounter substantial production costs and sequence variability, accentuating the urgent requirement for targeted small-molecule therapeutics. To bypass the complications of antigenic drift observed in viral surface glycoproteins, researchers focused on the nucleocapsid protein, an indispensable structural component of human metapneumovirus. The single-stranded negative-sense RNA viral genome encodes nine proteins, including structural and nonstructural elements such as the fusion protein, attachment glycoprotein, small hydrophobic protein, matrix protein, large RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, phosphoprotein, and two nonstructural factors. The nucleocapsid protein plays a foundational role in safeguarding viral genetic material by encasing genomic RNA, preventing host immune recognition, and forming an active ribonucleoprotein replication complex alongside the viral phosphoprotein cofactor and the large polymerase enzyme. Because the nucleocapsid sequence is highly conserved across strains and serves an obligatory mechanical function in genomic encapsidation and transcriptional elongation, it represents an especially attractive antiviral target, as disruption of its binding interactions could suppress viral propagation and diminish overall clinical disease severity. The investigative team established a structured computational pipeline that integrated structure-based virtual screening, secondary redocking, continuous five-hundred-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations, free energy calculations, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion predictions. Structural modeling was anchored to the high-resolution crystal structure of the monomeric, RNA-free human metapneumovirus nucleocapsid protein bound to its phosphoprotein cofactor, cataloged under Protein Data Bank identifier 5FVD at a resolution of 1.86 angstroms. Preparation of the macromolecule was executed using the DockPrep utility within UCSF Chimera, wherein crystallographic water molecules were cleared, polar hydrogens were added, protonation states of active-site residues were inspected, and energetic minimization was conducted to relieve steric clashes. Binding cavity coordinates were computed using the CASTp server, prioritizing the largest predicted pocket which incorporates functional amino acid residues such as leucine 167, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, and methionine 337 that participate directly in RNA association and nucleoprotein oligomerization. The screening scores across the library spanned an energetic spectrum from minus 10.7 to positive 8.3 kilocalories per mole. From this initial assessment, the three top-ranked candidate structures were shortlisted for secondary redocking using AutoDock Vina in UCSF Chimera alongside Gamma-Fagarine, a compound selected as a comparative reference standard due to its established antiviral relevance and baseline interaction stability within the target pocket. The three candidate compounds—designated by identifiers 24,330,502, 24,292,974, and 17,515,455—exhibited primary virtual screening scores of minus 10.7, minus 10.3, and minus 10.3 kilocalories per mole, substantially surpassing the reference molecule. Secondary redocking analyses validated the docking consistency of the shortlisted molecules, yielding binding energies of minus 10.2 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,330,502, minus 10.3 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,292,974, and minus 9.6 kilocalories per mole for compound 17,515,455. In contrast, Gamma-Fagarine produced a noticeably weaker redocking score of minus 6.3 kilocalories per mole, suggesting a diminished capacity for binding site occupancy. Compound 24,292,974 corresponds to PubChem identifier 4292500, chemically named N-(2-(4-fluorophenyl)-4,6-dihydro-2H-thieno[3,4-c]pyrazol-3-yl)-2-oxo-2H-chromene-3-carboxamide, while compound 17,515,455 corresponds to PubChem identifier 7125864, identified as 4-benzyl-1-(4-fluorophenyl)-[1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinazolin-5(4H)-one. The reference standard Gamma-Fagarine is recorded under PubChem identifier 107936. Discover more Get Rapid Tests Meet Dietitians Track Biotech Detailed intermolecular contact mapping carried out with the Desmond and Maestro visualization modules demonstrated intricate noncovalent interaction networks that anchored the candidate ligands within the nucleocapsid binding groove. Compound 24,330,502 established an extensive hydrophobic network involving leucine 167, isoleucine 176, valine 178, alanine 254, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, isoleucine 335, and methionine 337, complemented by prominent pi-pi stacking interactions with tryptophan 261. Compound 24,292,974 developed direct hydrogen bonds with threonine 170 and serine 174, while also engaging hydrophobic contacts with leucine 167, isoleucine 176, valine 178, alanine 254, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, and isoleucine 335, alongside dual pi-pi stacking and cation-pi interactions involving arginine 186 and tryptophan 261. Compound 17,515,455 anchored through a hydrogen bond with threonine 257, an extensive hydrophobic assembly with residues including leucine 167, alanine 254, and methionine 337, and both pi-pi stacking and cation-pi associations with arginine 186 and tryptophan 261. By comparison, Gamma-Fagarine established hydrogen bonds with serine 174, threonine 257, and arginine 260, but engaged fewer hydrophobic contacts and lacked pi-pi stacking altogether. To evaluate the conformational behavior and kinetic stability of the complexes under simulated physiological conditions, unconstrained five-hundred-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations were conducted using Desmond and Maestro with the OPLS-2005 force field. Each solvated system was enclosed in an orthorhombic periodic boundary box of TIP3P water molecules with ten angstroms of buffer clearance, neutralized through sodium and chloride counter-ions, and adjusted to 0.15 molar sodium chloride. Systems underwent two-stage energy minimization followed by consecutive NVT equilibration at 300 Kelvin via Berendsen thermostats and NPT equilibration at one atmosphere utilizing Nosé-Hoover thermostats and Martyna-Tobias-Klein barostats. Particle mesh Ewald summations governed electrostatic forces, with van der Waals cutoffs established at ten angstroms, recording trajectories every ten picoseconds over the five-hundred-nanosecond production phase. Root mean square deviation trajectories confirmed that the top candidate complexes attained structural equilibrium across the simulation timeframe. The complex formed by compound 24,330,502 demonstrated exceptional stability, maintaining low protein and ligand root mean square deviation values below four angstroms with minimal fluctuations throughout the trajectory. Compound 24,292,974 displayed a steady protein backbone but exhibited ligand deviations that reached up to twelve angstroms, indicating dynamic conformational adjustments within the cavity. Compound 17,515,455 maintained steady coordinates before undergoing a minor deviation shift near four hundred nanoseconds consistent with localized ligand repositioning. Conversely, the Gamma-Fagarine complex exhibited profound instability, with ligand deviations surpassing thirty angstroms, reflecting weak target retention and progressive dissociation from the binding pocket. Complementary root mean square fluctuation analyses of protein residues and ligand coordinates affirmed that critical amino acids forming the binding pocket experienced minimal atomic deviation, although terminal protein segments exhibited expected flexibility. While compound 24,292,974 and compound 17,515,455 displayed moderate flexibility, the reference standard Gamma-Fagarine generated extreme fluctuations ranging between twelve and fifteen angstroms. Principal component analysis substantiated these dynamics across the first two eigenvectors, which accounted for substantial variance proportions. Projections for compound 24,330,502, whose first two principal components captured 54.1 percent and 15.1 percent of variance respectively, formed compact, well-defined clusters indicative of homogenous structural sampling. In contrast, Gamma-Fagarine generated widely dispersed projections spanning 56.0 percent and 18.2 percent of variance, denoting extensive structural transitions and lack of stable complexation. Thermodynamic stability was further interrogated through free energy landscape construction and structural superimposition of representative low-energy conformations against initial docked coordinates. Free energy landscape projections generated via the Geo-Measures plugin revealed that compound 24,330,502 resided within a deep, singular, concentrated energy basin, reflecting a stable state. Compounds 24,292,974 and 17,515,455 navigated multiple shallow energy minima representing permissible conformational flexibility, whereas Gamma-Fagarine yielded fragmented, shallow basins characteristic of unstable binding. Superimposition of the lowest-energy conformations extracted from simulation trajectories demonstrated minimal structural drift from original docking coordinates, yielding root mean square deviations of 1.928 angstroms for compound 24,330,502, 1.722 angstroms for compound 24,292,974, and 2.029 angstroms for compound 17,515,455, compared with 1.855 angstroms for Gamma-Fagarine. End-point binding free energy calculations performed using the Prime MM/GBSA method over the final fifty nanoseconds of trajectory confirmed robust thermodynamic affinities for the candidate molecules. Compound 17,515,455 achieved the most favorable net binding free energy of minus 74.57 plus or minus 7.81 kilocalories per mole, followed by compound 24,330,502 at minus 68.83 plus or minus 4.47 kilocalories per mole, and compound 24,292,974 at minus 45.75 plus or minus 3.61 kilocalories per mole. In stark contrast, Gamma-Fagarine yielded a significantly weaker binding free energy of minus 24.89 plus or minus 2.28 kilocalories per mole. Energetic decomposition highlighted that nonpolar forces drove complexation, with van der Waals contributions reaching minus 54.52 kilocalories per mole for compound 17,515,455 and minus 53.73 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,330,502. These were reinforced by favorable lipophilic free energies of minus 26.79 plus or minus 1.56 and minus 21.01 plus or minus 1.09 kilocalories per mole, alongside favorable electrostatic contributions for compounds 24,330,502 and 17,515,455. Pharmacokinetic and physicochemical evaluations using SwissADME revealed generally favorable drug-likeness profiles alongside specific liabilities that direct future lead optimization. All three candidate compounds demonstrated high predicted gastrointestinal absorption, absence of pan-assay interference compounds structural alerts, and identical bioavailability scores of 0.55. Compounds 24,330,502 and 24,292,974 satisfied Lipinski rule-of-five criteria with zero violations, while compound 17,515,455 exhibited a single violation. Synthetic accessibility scores ranged favorably from 2.90 to 3.57. However, the profiling flagged several optimization requirements: compounds 24,330,502 and 17,515,455 showed predicted blood-brain barrier permeability, multiple cytochrome P450 isoenzyme inhibition liabilities across CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4 were identified, and moderate to poor aqueous solubility classifications were recorded across thermodynamic descriptors. Crucially, the authors emphasized that these computational observations are strictly in silico predictions that cannot capture physiological complexity, requiring subsequent in vitro biophysical assays, surface plasmon resonance binding studies, cytotoxicity profiling, and cell-culture validation to confirm therapeutic efficacy against live human metapneumovirus. elements_en.time: A computational study was published on November 24, 2026, with the investigation conducted to identify small molecules targeting the nucleocapsid protein of human metapneumovirus.
elements_en.location_and_population: The study is globally relevant, as human metapneumovirus is a leading cause of acute respiratory tract infections across all demographics, particularly affecting pediatric, elderly, and immunocompromised populations.
elements_en.event: A computational drug discovery investigation identified three candidate small-molecule inhibitors that demonstrate favorable binding affinity, structural stability, and drug-like properties against the nucleocapsid protein of human metapneumovirus. The study was reported by Bioengineer.org.
elements_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Human metapneumovirus causes significant morbidity, with seasonal outbreaks circulating globally and seroprevalence surveys indicating widespread infection by age five. There are currently no approved antiviral therapies or protective vaccines directed against the pathogen, highlighting the urgent need for targeted small-molecule therapeutics.
elements_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study outlines a computational pipeline that includes structure-based virtual screening, molecular dynamics simulations, and binding energy calculations. The findings are based on in silico methods and are not yet validated through clinical trials or real-world application.

news.title_zh: 计算研究确定了靶向 人偏肺病毒 核衣壳的候选小分子 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: A computational study published on November 24, 2026, identified three candidate small-molecule inhibitors targeting the nucleocapsid protein of human metapneumovirus. The research, conducted by an investigative team, focused on overcoming challenges posed by antigenic drift in viral surface glycoproteins by targeting the nucleocapsid, which is highly conserved across strains. The study used a structured pipeline involving virtual screening, molecular dynamics simulations, and binding energy calculations. The three top-ranked compounds—24,330,502, 24,292,974, and 17,515,455—exhibited strong docking affinity and stability, surpassing the reference compound Gamma-Fagarine. These findings highlight the potential for developing targeted antiviral therapies against human metapneumovirus, which remains a significant cause of respiratory infections, particularly in vulnerable populations such as children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. However, the results are based on in silico methods and require further validation through clinical trials before they can be applied in real-world scenarios.
news.content_zh: 2026 年 11 月 24 日发表的一项计算研究确定了三种针对 人偏肺病毒 核衣壳蛋白的候选小分子抑制剂。这项研究由一个研究小组进行,重点是通过针对跨病毒株高度保守的核衣壳来克服病毒表面糖蛋白抗原漂移带来的挑战。该研究使用了涉及虚拟筛选、分子动力学模拟和结合能计算的结构化流程。排名靠前的三种化合物——24,330,502、24,292,974 和 17,515,455——表现出强大的对接亲和力和稳定性,超过了参考化合物 Gamma-Fagarine。这些发现凸显了开发针对 人偏肺病毒 的靶向 抗病毒药物 疗法的潜力,人偏肺病毒 仍然是呼吸道感染的一个重要原因,特别是在儿童、老年人和免疫功能低下的个体等弱势群体中。然而,结果是基于计算机方法,需要通过临床试验进一步验证,然后才能应用于现实场景。

news.content_title: 除了流感,最近还有一种病毒需要留意
news.content: 除了流感,最近还有一种病毒需要留意 儿科林医生 2026-11-20 18:05发布于广东怡禾医疗儿科医生 问AI · 检测手段进步怎样揭开偏肺病毒的面纱? 昨天(11月19日),中国疾病预防控制中心发布了今年第46周的急性呼吸道传染病哨点监测数据。 除了大家近期比较关注的流感,还有一种病毒的检测阳性率也在逐渐上升,那就是人偏肺病毒(Human metapneumovirus,HMPV)。 在过去5周里,人偏肺病毒在门急诊流感样病例中的检测阳性率从3.7%升至5.5%,在住院严重急性呼吸道感染病例中则从3.5%升至6.8%。[1] 尤其是在5岁以下的住院严重急性呼吸道感染患儿中,人偏肺病毒的检测阳性率已经排到了第二位,仅次于鼻病毒。[1] 相比流感病毒、呼吸道合胞病毒,相信很多人对人偏肺病毒还比较陌生。 这是新发现的病毒吗?严重吗?要怎么治疗? 一、人偏肺病毒是什么? 人偏肺病毒跟呼吸道合胞病毒一样,都属于肺病毒科,不过它是偏肺病毒属,是一种有包膜的单股负链RNA病毒。[2] 这不是最近才发现的新病毒。事实上,早在2001年就已经被荷兰学者发现,而且,血清学研究表明,早在20世纪50年代,这种病毒就已经在人群中传播了。[3,4] 之所以大家以前很少听说这个病毒,在一定程度上与检测手段有关。随着分子诊断技术的普及,越来越多的呼吸道感染能够明确具体的病原体,人偏肺病毒也因此逐渐被大家所认识。[4] 二、哪些人更容易感染? 所有人都容易感染。绝大多数人其实在婴幼儿期就已经感染过这个病毒,但感染后并不会产生永久性的免疫保护,所以反复感染是很常见的。[2-4] 相对来说,幼儿、老年人以及免疫功能低下人群,更容易在感染后出现重症表现。[2,5] 三、感染后会引起什么问题? 和其他呼吸道病毒类似,人偏肺病毒感染后主要是引起呼吸道症状,从上至下,无所不及,比如普通感冒、喉炎、毛细支气管炎、肺炎,后两者也是导致儿童感染后住院的最常见原因。[2,4,5] 儿童感染后的常见症状包括咳嗽、流涕、发热、喘息等。成人的症状也大致相似。[2,4,5] 当然,并不是所有人感染后都会出现症状,也有些幸运儿是无症状感染者。[2] 四、做什么检查才知道是否感染? 核酸。 核酸是检测有无人偏肺病毒感染最简单方便准确的方法,现在很多大医院都可以做,甚至美团、京东在不少大城市也开展了相关的快检服务。[2,4,5] 不过,并不是所有孩子出现呼吸道感染症状,都有必要做这项检查。对于症状较轻的孩子,由于目前没有针对人偏肺病毒的特效药,是否明确感染了这种病毒,通常不会改变治疗方案。[4,5] 至于血清抗体、血常规,都不适合作为常规确诊人偏肺病毒急性感染的检查。[2] 血常规对判断是否细菌或病毒感染本来就没有多大帮助,更判断不了是什么病毒感染。 至于血清抗体,由于感染后抗体可以持续存在较长时间,单次抗体检测阳性也可能只是提示既往感染,不能据此确诊当前感染。大多数儿童在5岁时就已经感染过人偏肺病毒。[2,3] 五、感染了要用什么药? 目前尚无获批用于治疗人偏肺病毒感染的特异性抗病毒药物,也不建议常规使用利巴韦林、干扰素等药物。如果没有合并细菌感染的证据,也不需要使用抗生素。[2,4-6] 即便如此,我们也不用担心,因为人偏肺病毒感染后一般都是可以自愈的,所以我们只需要做好必要的对症支持处理就行。 比如发热引起不适时使用退热药(如布洛芬或对乙酰氨基酚),喉炎合并喉梗阻时可能需要使用激素,注意保证水分摄入和休息充足等。[5,6] 大多数轻症患者在1周左右症状会逐渐缓解,不过咳嗽可能持续更长时间。[6] 如果孩子出现呼吸急促、呼吸费力、精神状态明显变差、进食或饮水困难、持续高热超过3天等情况,则需及时就医。对于小月龄婴儿、有慢性心肺疾病或免疫功能低下的孩子,就医的门槛可以适当降低。[2,5,6] 六、感染后要隔离多久? 目前我国尚未将人偏肺病毒感染单独列入甲、乙、丙类传染病目录,也没有针对普通患儿的全国统一返学时间标准。[7] 儿童感染后,病毒核酸可持续检出数日至数周,但核酸阳性并不意味着仍具有传染性。[8] 一般来说,如果孩子已经在不使用退热药的情况下体温都能保持正常,同时呼吸道症状整体有所好转,持续至少24小时,且身体状况允许正常参加学校活动,就可以考虑返学。[9] 不需要等到咳嗽、流鼻涕等症状完全消失,也不需要常规复查核酸直至阴性。[9] 七、如何预防感染? 针对人偏肺病毒的疫苗目前仍在研发中,尚未获批上市,所以暂时我们还没办法通过接种疫苗这一有效方法来预防感染。[4,5] 考虑到人偏肺病毒可通过感染者排出的呼吸道颗粒、密切接触,以及接触被病毒污染的物品后触摸口、鼻、眼等途径传播。因此,我们可以采取以下措施来降低感染风险:[4,5] 注意勤洗手; 保持室内良好通风; 在人员密集或通风不良的场所科学佩戴口罩; 尽量避免与有呼吸道感染症状的人密切接触; 生病期间尽量居家休息,减少传染给他人的机会。 最后,关于人偏肺病毒,你还有其他问题吗?又或者,你或孩子感染过吗? news.content_original: 除了流感,最近还有一种病毒需要留意 儿科林医生 2026-11-20 18:05发布于广东怡禾医疗儿科医生 问AI · 检测手段进步怎样揭开偏肺病毒的面纱? 昨天(11月19日),中国疾病预防控制中心发布了今年第46周的急性呼吸道传染病哨点监测数据。 除了大家近期比较关注的流感,还有一种病毒的检测阳性率也在逐渐上升,那就是人偏肺病毒(Human metapneumovirus,HMPV)。 在过去5周里,人偏肺病毒在门急诊流感样病例中的检测阳性率从3.7%升至5.5%,在住院严重急性呼吸道感染病例中则从3.5%升至6.8%。[1] 尤其是在5岁以下的住院严重急性呼吸道感染患儿中,人偏肺病毒的检测阳性率已经排到了第二位,仅次于鼻病毒。[1] 相比流感病毒、呼吸道合胞病毒,相信很多人对人偏肺病毒还比较陌生。 这是新发现的病毒吗?严重吗?要怎么治疗? 一、人偏肺病毒是什么? 人偏肺病毒跟呼吸道合胞病毒一样,都属于肺病毒科,不过它是偏肺病毒属,是一种有包膜的单股负链RNA病毒。[2] 这不是最近才发现的新病毒。事实上,早在2001年就已经被荷兰学者发现,而且,血清学研究表明,早在20世纪50年代,这种病毒就已经在人群中传播了。[3,4] 之所以大家以前很少听说这个病毒,在一定程度上与检测手段有关。随着分子诊断技术的普及,越来越多的呼吸道感染能够明确具体的病原体,人偏肺病毒也因此逐渐被大家所认识。[4] 二、哪些人更容易感染? 所有人都容易感染。绝大多数人其实在婴幼儿期就已经感染过这个病毒,但感染后并不会产生永久性的免疫保护,所以反复感染是很常见的。[2-4] 相对来说,幼儿、老年人以及免疫功能低下人群,更容易在感染后出现重症表现。[2,5] 三、感染后会引起什么问题? 和其他呼吸道病毒类似,人偏肺病毒感染后主要是引起呼吸道症状,从上至下,无所不及,比如普通感冒、喉炎、毛细支气管炎、肺炎,后两者也是导致儿童感染后住院的最常见原因。[2,4,5] 儿童感染后的常见症状包括咳嗽、流涕、发热、喘息等。成人的症状也大致相似。[2,4,5] 当然,并不是所有人感染后都会出现症状,也有些幸运儿是无症状感染者。[2] 四、做什么检查才知道是否感染? 核酸。 核酸是检测有无人偏肺病毒感染最简单方便准确的方法,现在很多大医院都可以做,甚至美团、京东在不少大城市也开展了相关的快检服务。[2,4,5] 不过,并不是所有孩子出现呼吸道感染症状,都有必要做这项检查。对于症状较轻的孩子,由于目前没有针对人偏肺病毒的特效药,是否明确感染了这种病毒,通常不会改变治疗方案。[4,5] 至于血清抗体、血常规,都不适合作为常规确诊人偏肺病毒急性感染的检查。[2] 血常规对判断是否细菌或病毒感染本来就没有多大帮助,更判断不了是什么病毒感染。 至于血清抗体,由于感染后抗体可以持续存在较长时间,单次抗体检测阳性也可能只是提示既往感染,不能据此确诊当前感染。大多数儿童在5岁时就已经感染过人偏肺病毒。[2,3] 五、感染了要用什么药? 目前尚无获批用于治疗人偏肺病毒感染的特异性抗病毒药物,也不建议常规使用利巴韦林、干扰素等药物。如果没有合并细菌感染的证据,也不需要使用抗生素。[2,4-6] 即便如此,我们也不用担心,因为人偏肺病毒感染后一般都是可以自愈的,所以我们只需要做好必要的对症支持处理就行。 比如发热引起不适时使用退热药(如布洛芬或对乙酰氨基酚),喉炎合并喉梗阻时可能需要使用激素,注意保证水分摄入和休息充足等。[5,6] 大多数轻症患者在1周左右症状会逐渐缓解,不过咳嗽可能持续更长时间。[6] 如果孩子出现呼吸急促、呼吸费力、精神状态明显变差、进食或饮水困难、持续高热超过3天等情况,则需及时就医。对于小月龄婴儿、有慢性心肺疾病或免疫功能低下的孩子,就医的门槛可以适当降低。[2,5,6] 六、感染后要隔离多久? 目前我国尚未将人偏肺病毒感染单独列入甲、乙、丙类传染病目录,也没有针对普通患儿的全国统一返学时间标准。[7] 儿童感染后,病毒核酸可持续检出数日至数周,但核酸阳性并不意味着仍具有传染性。[8] 一般来说,如果孩子已经在不使用退热药的情况下体温都能保持正常,同时呼吸道症状整体有所好转,持续至少24小时,且身体状况允许正常参加学校活动,就可以考虑返学。[9] 不需要等到咳嗽、流鼻涕等症状完全消失,也不需要常规复查核酸直至阴性。[9] 七、如何预防感染? 针对人偏肺病毒的疫苗目前仍在研发中,尚未获批上市,所以暂时我们还没办法通过接种疫苗这一有效方法来预防感染。[4,5] 考虑到人偏肺病毒可通过感染者排出的呼吸道颗粒、密切接触,以及接触被病毒污染的物品后触摸口、鼻、眼等途径传播。因此,我们可以采取以下措施来降低感染风险:[4,5] 注意勤洗手; 保持室内良好通风; 在人员密集或通风不良的场所科学佩戴口罩; 尽量避免与有呼吸道感染症状的人密切接触; 生病期间尽量居家休息,减少传染给他人的机会。 最后,关于人偏肺病毒,你还有其他问题吗?又或者,你或孩子感染过吗? 欢迎留言分享你的经历~ 参考资料: [1] 中国疾病预防控制中心. 全国急性呼吸道传染病哨点监测情况(2026年第42~46周). [2] 中华医学会儿科学分会呼吸学组,国家呼吸系统疾病临床医学研究中心, 国家感染与过敏性疾病临床医学监测中心. 人偏肺病毒感染诊断、治疗和预防指南[J]. 中华实用儿科临床杂志, 2025, 40(8): 561-570. [3] van den Hoogen BG, de Jong JC, Groen J, et al. analysis.brief_en: The article highlights the increasing detection rate of human metapneumovirus (HMPV) in China, particularly among hospitalized children with severe acute respiratory infections. According to data from the National Center for Disease Control and Prevention, the positivity rate of HMPV in outpatient flu-like cases rose from 3.7% to 5.5%, and in hospitalized severe acute respiratory infection cases, it increased from 3.5% to 6.8%. In children under five, HMPV is the second most common cause of hospitalization, following rhinovirus. The article explains that HMPV is not a newly discovered virus but has been known since 2001, with evidence of circulation dating back to the 1950s. It emphasizes that while there is no specific antiviral treatment, most cases are self-limiting, requiring only symptomatic care. Preventive measures include hand hygiene, ventilation, mask-wearing in crowded places, and avoiding close contact with infected individuals. The article also notes that there is no national standard for returning to school for children infected with HMPV, and that the virus is not classified as a statutory infectious disease in China.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Surveillance in Bangkok Reveals Influenza and Rhinovirus Dominated 2025 Respiratory Infections by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Surveillance in Bangkok Reveals Influenza and Rhinovirus Dominated 2025 Respiratory Infections Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective surveillance investigation conducted across 2025 in Bangkok, Thailand, identified respiratory viruses in 61.1 percent of patients evaluated for acute respiratory infections. Analyzing 4,697 nasopharyngeal specimens from individuals presenting with acute respiratory symptoms at Bangpakok 9 International Hospital, investigators identified 2,871 positive samples containing 3,151 viral detections. Influenza virus was the predominant pathogen, registering an overall detection rate of 22.2 percent across all tested samples. Human rhinovirus represented the second most frequent agent at 16.6 percent, while SARS-CoV-2 accounted for 9.9 percent of cases. Single-pathogen detections constituted 55.4 percent of samples, whereas multivirus coinfections were confirmed in 5.7 percent of patients. Screening eight viral targets across twelve months established an empirical baseline of viral transmission across patients ranging from one month to 97 years old. Acute respiratory infections represent an enduring public health burden, causing substantial hospitalizations and mortality across all age groups, particularly young children and the elderly. Pathogen diversity is extensive, involving influenza virus, human rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, SARS-CoV-2, human parainfluenza virus, human metapneumovirus, human coronavirus, and human adenovirus. Infection severity depends on pathogen type, coinfections, age, and underlying comorbidities. In tropical settings like Thailand, climatic and geographic factors create circulation dynamics that differ markedly from temperate zones, where infections peak primarily during winter.
