news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Multi-Method Statistical Analysis Maps Interacting Spread of Co-Circulating Respiratory Viruses by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Multi-Method Statistical Analysis Maps Interacting Spread of Co-Circulating Respiratory Viruses Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive statistical investigation analyzing laboratory-confirmed surveillance records across three epidemiological seasons has identified consistent, directional patterns of statistical association among major co-circulating respiratory viruses. Utilizing high-resolution incidence data gathered between October 2022 and May 2025, researchers examined how weekly fluctuations in the spread of individual pathogens statistically correlate with, precede, or trail the activity of others at both provincial and national scales. The resulting findings demonstrate that co-circulating respiratory pathogens do not transmit as entirely isolated entities within human populations. Instead, multi-model statistical assessments uncovered a reproducible network of both cooperative and competitive associations across varying time horizons. Several viral pairs exhibited persistent positive associations across independent analytical frameworks, such as between human metapneumovirus and parainfluenza virus or between human seasonal coronaviruses and influenza, whereas other pairings displayed recurring negative associations over extended time lags. By deploying an ensemble of complementary statistical methodologies, the investigation provides nuanced empirical documentation of how multiple acute respiratory pathogens simultaneously navigate host populations over successive seasonal epidemics. The public health motivation underlying this investigation stems from the substantial global burden imposed by acute respiratory infections, which represent leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. While many viral respiratory episodes present with mild symptomatology, infections frequently progress to severe outcomes including hospital admissions, long-term disability, and premature mortality, particularly among clinically vulnerable demographics. Seasonal influenza alone accounts for an estimated three to five million severe cases and up to 650,000 deaths across the globe annually, while respiratory syncytial virus generates approximately 33 million infections, over three million hospitalizations, and more than 100,000 pediatric deaths each year in children under the age of five. Acute respiratory infections markedly increase disability-adjusted life-years lost while depleting quality-adjusted life-years across populations. Controlling these diseases remains exceptionally difficult because co-circulating pathogens generate overlapping clinical presentations that cannot be distinguished through symptoms alone. Furthermore, complex host-level mechanisms, ranging from cross-protective heterologous immunity to adverse immune priming, combine with population-level social dynamics to alter transmission pathways, making comprehensive statistical evaluation of co-circulation vital for public health preparedness. To evaluate these dynamics empirically, the research team analyzed longitudinal surveillance data collected through Infectieradar, an opt-in participatory surveillance system administered by the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment. Operating across all twelve NUTS-2 provincial territories in the Netherlands, the platform collects weekly self-reported symptom data alongside basic health profiles, healthcare-seeking practices, and social contact behaviors from volunteer participants. A subset of symptomatic participants undergoes laboratory multiplex polymerase chain reaction testing, yielding verified pathogen-specific detections rather than broad community incidence or raw positivity rates. Between October 4, 2022, and May 12, 2025, the platform recorded 7,642 confirmed respiratory infections across three full epidemiological cycles running continuously through intermediate warmer months. The study focused on individuals aged twenty and older, stratified into age groups of 20 to 65 years and over 65 years, after excluding 167 entries lacking regional records and 43 cases from individuals under twenty due to sparse representation. The final data encompassed seven predominant viral groups: SARS-CoV-2, respiratory syncytial virus, influenza viruses, rhino- and enterovirus complex, human metapneumovirus, parainfluenza virus, and human seasonal coronaviruses. Discover more Engineering Job Board Research Paper Access Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges The analytical design implemented a tiered sequence of statistical methodologies to evaluate associations across distinct operational scales while addressing varying distributional assumptions. Initial exploratory evaluations deployed Granger causality tests within multivariate vector autoregressive structures alongside principal component analysis to assess temporal predictability and identify shared modes of temporal variation across provinces. To quantify contemporaneous associations while adjusting for demographic, geographic, and temporal confounders, the researchers constructed a hierarchical Bayesian latent Gaussian model with correlated residuals following negative binomial distributions. This latent Gaussian formulation incorporated pathogen-specific intercepts, regional random effects, smooth temporal spline baselines, and structured age effects parameterized using social contact matrices obtained from the Dutch POLYMOD social contact survey via the SOCRATES platform. By applying weakly informative Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe correlation priors and penalized complexity standard deviation priors, posterior correlations derived from the residual covariance matrix isolated contemporaneous synchronous variation among pathogens, distinguishing cooperative parallel surges from competitive residual divergence after controlling for shared structural drivers. To evaluate immediate temporal interactions, the investigators formulated three distinct generalized regression frameworks incorporating direct one-week lagged disease counts as predictors. Weekly regional counts stratified by age group were modeled under negative binomial assumptions using generalized linear mixed models, vector generalized linear models, and generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape. The generalized linear mixed model accounted for unobserved spatial heterogeneity through normally distributed regional random intercepts while applying a shared overdispersion parameter across all categories. In contrast, the vector generalized linear model represented regional differences as fixed effects while estimating pathogen-specific dispersion parameters to account for varying variance profiles among individual viruses. Extending this structure, the generalized additive model for location, scale, and shape jointly estimated both the mean count sub-model and pathogen-specific dispersion parameters. Across all three regression formulations, predictor sets incorporated one-week lagged incidence counts for every pathogen, regional indicators, age brackets, harmonic seasonal sine and cosine terms, and natural cubic splines to adjust for background temporal trajectories. Recognizing that observed associations might arise from divergent transmission dynamics, the authors implemented an endemic-epidemic statistical formulation to decouple baseline background circulation from autoregressive transmission processes. This framework partitions expected weekly disease counts into an endemic component, capturing persistent exogenous factors such as climate-driven seasonality and susceptible replenishment, and an epidemic component, capturing localized transmission driven by autoregressive feedback and spatial contact structures. The research team explored structural specifications incorporating one-week lagged counts of alternate pathogens into the endemic sub-model, the epidemic sub-model, or simultaneously within both components. Across all examined respiratory pathogens, fitted model estimates indicated that the endemic baseline accounted for more than ninety percent of total incidence for respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, and parainfluenza virus. Conversely, the autoregressive epidemic component contributed fifteen to twenty percent of incidence for influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and human coronaviruses, reaching nearly forty percent for the rhino- and enterovirus complex. To capture delayed and nonlinear dependencies operating beyond immediate weekly lags, the researchers integrated distributed lag nonlinear models within the vector generalized linear regression framework. This approach mapped the influence of past pathogen activity across exposure intensity and delayed temporal intervals using smooth bivariate cross-basis functions. Exposure dimensions were parameterized using linear basis functions, while lag dimensions utilized degree-one B-spline functions evaluated across extended lag windows reaching up to eight weeks. The resulting lag-response surfaces quantified relative risks at specified exposure levels across multi-week delays, revealing whether associations exhibited delayed peaks or temporal shifts in directional sign. Furthermore, the distributed lag methodology was applied to examine lineage- and subtype-level dynamics within specific pathogen families. Across the complementary statistical modeling frameworks, several prominent and reproducible associations emerged from the empirical surveillance record. In one-week lagged regression analyses, human metapneumovirus exhibited a consistent positive association with subsequent parainfluenza virus activity across all three regression models, yielding mean incidence rate ratios of 1.3259 in the mixed model, 1.6629 in the vector generalized model, and 1.2998 in the generalized additive model. Similarly, human seasonal coronavirus showed a robust positive association with influenza virus, a finding reinforced within both the endemic and epidemic tiers of the endemic-epidemic model and peaking at lag four in distributed lag modeling with a relative risk of 1.2962. Conversely, a recurrent competitive relationship was observed between influenza and subsequent rhino- and enterovirus activity, demonstrating significant negative incidence rate ratios across all three regression frameworks and depressed relative risks in distributed lag models. Contemporaneous latent Gaussian residuals likewise identified strong positive correlation between influenza and respiratory syncytial virus alongside negative correlation between influenza and parainfluenza virus. Subtype-level distributed lag analyses further illuminated intricate intra-family and lineage-specific patterns that were masked when pathogens were aggregated into broad classifications. Within coronaviruses, human seasonal coronavirus NL63/HKU1 displayed persistent positive associations with subsequent SARS-CoV-2 detections across all examined lags, whereas human coronavirus 229E demonstrated significant negative associations with SARS-CoV-2 at lags spanning five to seven weeks. These diverse lagged patterns highlight marked directional asymmetry: the statistical influence of pathogen A preceding pathogen B frequently differed in sign, magnitude, and temporal duration from the reverse sequence. Multicollinearity stemming from overlapping seasonal epidemic peaks was mitigated across models by incorporating explicit seasonal harmonic smoothers and autoregressive components, ensuring that identified associations reflected robust lagged correlations rather than synchronized seasonal peaks. The study authors emphasize critical methodological boundaries, cautioning that all identified relationships represent statistical associations within observational surveillance data rather than proven biological interactions or direct clinical causality. Because testing within Infectieradar requires participants to experience respiratory symptoms, shared propensity for testing among symptomatic individuals introduces potential sampling selection biases that can generate apparent synchrony. Furthermore, the opt-in participatory cohort is not fully representative of the general Dutch population, weekly laboratory sampling capacity was capped at fixed thresholds, and children under twenty years old were excluded from primary model fittings. Additionally, post-pandemic population dynamics, including altered baseline immunity resulting from earlier non-pharmaceutical interventions, may have temporarily modified seasonal circulation patterns throughout the observation window. Nonetheless, by demonstrating consistent statistical associations across distinct regression, latent variable, and distributed lag frameworks, this multi-model investigation establishes a rigorous, adaptable epidemiological foundation for interpreting multi-pathogen surveillance data and optimizing respiratory disease monitoring strategies. Across all examined respiratory pathogens, fitted model estimates indicated that the endemic baseline accounted for more than ninety percent of total incidence for respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, and parainfluenza virus. Conversely, the autoregressive epidemic component contributed fifteen to twenty percent of incidence for influenza, SARS-CoV-2, and human coronaviruses, reaching nearly forty percent for the rhino- and enterovirus complex. To capture delayed and nonlinear dependencies operating beyond immediate weekly lags, the researchers integrated distributed lag nonlinear models within the vector generalized linear regression framework. This approach mapped the influence of past pathogen activity across exposure intensity and delayed temporal intervals using smooth bivariate cross-basis functions. Exposure dimensions were parameterized using linear basis functions, while lag dimensions utilized degree-one B-spline functions evaluated across extended lag windows reaching up to eight weeks. The resulting lag-response surfaces quantified relative risks at specified exposure levels across multi-week delays, revealing whether associations exhibited delayed peaks or temporal shifts in directional sign. Furthermore, the distributed lag methodology was applied to examine lineage- and subtype-level dynamics within specific pathogen families. Across the complementary statistical modeling frameworks, several prominent and reproducible associations emerged from the empirical surveillance record. In one-week lagged regression analyses, human metapneumovirus exhibited a consistent positive association with subsequent parainfluenza virus activity across all three regression models, yielding mean incidence rate ratios of 1.3259 in the mixed model, 1.6629 in the vector generalized model, and 1.2998 in the generalized additive model. Similarly, human seasonal coronavirus showed a robust positive association with influenza virus, a finding reinforced within both the endemic and epidemic tiers of the endemic-epidemic model and peaking at lag four in distributed lag modeling with a relative risk of 1.2962. Conversely, a recurrent competitive relationship was observed between influenza and subsequent rhino- and enterovirus activity, demonstrating significant negative incidence rate ratios across all three regression frameworks and depressed relative risks in distributed lag models. Contemporaneous latent Gaussian residuals likewise identified strong positive correlation between influenza and respiratory syncytial virus alongside negative correlation between influenza and parainfluenza virus. Subtype-level distributed lag analyses further illuminated intricate intra-family and lineage-specific patterns that were masked when pathogens were aggregated into broad classifications. Within coronaviruses, human seasonal coronavirus NL63/HKU1 displayed persistent positive associations with subsequent SARS-CoV-2 detections across all examined lags, whereas human coronavirus 229E demonstrated significant negative associations with SARS-CoV-2 at lags spanning five to seven weeks. These diverse lagged patterns highlight marked directional asymmetry: the statistical influence of pathogen A preceding pathogen B frequently differed in sign, magnitude, and temporal duration from the reverse sequence. Multicollinearity stemming from overlapping seasonal epidemic peaks was mitigated across models by incorporating explicit seasonal harmonic smoothers and autoregressive components, ensuring that identified associations reflected robust lagged correlations rather than synchronized seasonal peaks. The study authors emphasize critical methodological boundaries, cautioning that all identified relationships represent statistical associations within observational surveillance data rather than proven biological interactions or direct clinical causality. Because testing within Infectieradar requires participants to experience respiratory symptoms, shared propensity for testing among symptomatic individuals introduces potential sampling selection biases that can generate apparent synchrony. Furthermore, the opt-in participatory cohort is not fully representative of the general Dutch population, weekly laboratory sampling capacity was capped at fixed thresholds, and children under twenty years old were excluded from primary model fittings. Additionally, post-pandemic population dynamics, including altered baseline immunity resulting from earlier non-pharmaceutical interventions, may have temporarily modified seasonal circulation patterns throughout the observation window. Nonetheless, by demonstrating consistent statistical associations across distinct regression, latent variable, and distributed lag frameworks, this multi-model investigation establishes a rigorous, adaptable epidemiological foundation for interpreting multi-pathogen surveillance data and optimizing respiratory disease monitoring strategies. analysis.time: The study analyzed data from October 2022 to May 2025, with the publication date being November 25, 2026. The findings were based on three full epidemiological cycles running continuously through intermediate warmer months.
analysis.location_and_population: The research was conducted in the Netherlands, specifically across all twelve NUTS-2 provincial territories. The study focused on individuals aged twenty and older, stratified into age groups of 20 to 65 years and over 65 years.
analysis.event: A multi-method statistical analysis was conducted to map the interacting spread of co-circulating respiratory viruses, including human metapneumovirus, across three epidemiological seasons. The study identified consistent, directional patterns of statistical association among major respiratory viruses.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study found that co-circulating respiratory pathogens do not transmit as isolated entities. It highlighted persistent positive associations between human metapneumovirus and parainfluenza virus, as well as between human seasonal coronaviruses and influenza. Other pairings showed recurring negative associations over extended time lags. The research emphasized the difficulty of controlling these diseases due to overlapping clinical presentations and complex host-level mechanisms.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The investigation used an ensemble of complementary statistical methodologies, including Granger causality tests, principal component analysis, and hierarchical Bayesian latent Gaussian models. The study accounted for demographic, geographic, and temporal confounders. However, the opt-in participatory cohort is not fully representative of the general Dutch population, and weekly laboratory sampling capacity was capped at fixed thresholds.

analysis.brief_en: A multi-method statistical analysis conducted by researchers in the Netherlands between October 2022 and May 2025 mapped the interacting spread of co-circulating respiratory viruses, including human metapneumovirus. The study, published on November 25, 2026, identified consistent, directional patterns of statistical association among major respiratory viruses, such as persistent positive links between human metapneumovirus and parainfluenza virus, and between human seasonal coronaviruses and influenza. Other pairings showed recurring negative associations over time lags. The research emphasized the challenges of controlling these diseases due to overlapping clinical presentations and complex host-level mechanisms. The investigation used advanced statistical methods, including Granger causality tests and hierarchical Bayesian models, to evaluate associations while adjusting for demographic, geographic, and temporal factors. However, the study's opt-in participatory cohort is not fully representative of the general Dutch population, and weekly laboratory sampling capacity was capped at fixed thresholds.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Rhinovirus Dominated Respiratory Infections Among Returning Iranian Pilgrims During 2025 Gatherings by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Rhinovirus Dominated Respiratory Infections Among Returning Iranian Pilgrims During 2025 Gatherings Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Rhinovirus emerged as the predominant respiratory pathogen detected among symptomatic Iranian pilgrims returning from both the Hajj and the Arbaeen walk in 2025, according to a molecular surveillance study published in Tropical Diseases, Travel Medicine and Vaccines. Conducted by researchers at the National Influenza Center within the School of Public Health at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, the investigation revealed marked differences in overall viral positivity and pathogen distribution between the two religious mass gathering cohorts. While rhinovirus remained the primary contributor to acute respiratory illness across both monitored groups, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) exhibited a pronounced disparity, presenting in only 1.7 percent of symptomatic Hajj travelers compared with 32 percent of those returning from the Arbaeen pilgrimage. The study cohort comprised 110 symptomatic Iranian pilgrims who underwent testing upon their return to Iran during the 2025 pilgrimage seasons, spanning an overall age range of 8 to 82 years. Among the participants, 60 had traveled to Mecca and Madinah, Saudi Arabia, for the annual Hajj pilgrimage, an event that drew approximately 86,700 Iranian travelers in 2025 alongside an estimated worldwide attendance of 3 million from more than 180 nations. The remaining 50 symptomatic participants were sampled following the Arbaeen walk in Iraq, where more than 21 million Iranian pilgrims took part in the traditional trek from Najaf to Karbala. Demographic profiling identified notable contrasts between the two mass gathering groups. The Hajj group consisted of 36 men (60 percent) and 24 women (40 percent), with a mean age of 58 ± 11.70 years and an age distribution ranging from 28 to 82 years. More than 80 percent of the surveyed Hajj travelers were older than 50 years. By comparison, the Arbaeen walk group included 37 men (74 percent) and 13 women (26 percent), with a substantially younger mean age of 35.18 ± 16.47 years, an age range spanning 8 to 68 years, and only 22 percent of participants aged over 50 years. These demographic records were compiled alongside diagnostic evaluations to assess how respiratory illness manifested across the distinct traveler populations. Discover more Get Cold Relief Check Symptoms infections Study Biology Infections To evaluate the viral spectrum, throat swab specimens collected from symptomatic travelers were processed at the National Influenza Center using standardized molecular extraction and detection protocols. Nucleic acid extraction was conducted using the magnetic-bead-based Zybio PRT DNA & RNA Extraction Kit. Multiplex detection was performed using the ARVI Screen Real-TM Sacace Biotechnologies Kit to identify human adenoviruses of species B, C, and E, human bocavirus, human rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, human metapneumovirus, human parainfluenza viruses 1 through 4, coronavirus 229E/NL63, and coronavirus OC43/HKU1. In parallel, standardized in-house qualitative real-time polymerase chain reaction assays using CDC-recommended primers and probes were employed to detect influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2, while testing for Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV) was conducted exclusively for returning Hajj pilgrims. Diagnostic results revealed an overall viral positivity rate of 30 percent among symptomatic Hajj pilgrims, with 18 of the 60 travelers testing positive for at least one respiratory pathogen. Rhinovirus was detected in 23.3 percent (14 of 60) of the Hajj participants, forming the largest share of identified infections. Betacoronavirus OC43/HKU1 was identified in 3.3 percent (2 of 60) of cases, while influenza A (H3N2) and SARS-CoV-2 were each detected at a low frequency of 1.7 percent (1 of 60). No cases of MERS-CoV were identified among the Hajj pilgrims, and no viral co-infections were detected within this cohort. In contrast, symptomatic Arbaeen walk travelers demonstrated a markedly higher overall positivity rate, with 78 percent (39 of 50) testing positive for at least one respiratory virus. Rhinovirus was once again the most frequently identified agent, found in 36 percent (18 of 50) of participants. SARS-CoV-2 was confirmed in 32 percent (16 of 50) of the Arbaeen cohort, representing a sharp elevation compared to the single case detected among Hajj travelers. Additionally, alphacoronavirus 229E/NL63 was identified in 6 percent (3 of 50), betacoronavirus OC43/HKU1 in 2 percent (1 of 50), and influenza B virus in 2 percent (1 of 50). Four Arbaeen participants, representing 8 percent of the group, presented with dual co-infections of rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2. Addressing the sharp difference in SARS-CoV-2 detection between the cohorts, the authors observed that the low 1.7 percent rate among Hajj travelers compared to 32 percent among Arbaeen travelers may correspond to divergences in preventive protocols, crowd density, or local healthcare environments. Specifically, COVID-19 vaccination was strongly recommended for Iranian pilgrims attending Hajj, whereas no corresponding vaccination policy was instituted for Arbaeen participants. However, the researchers emphasized that individual vaccination records and clinical severity data were unavailable, and variations in sampling procedures preclude direct causal comparisons regarding absolute transmission risk between the two mass gatherings. Both gatherings took place during the hot summer season under temperatures reaching up to 40 degrees Celsius, an environmental context traditionally associated with diminished transmission of seasonal influenza. This observation aligned with the very low frequencies of influenza detected in the study, contrasting sharply with historical data such as the 12.7 percent influenza prevalence recorded by Yavarian and colleagues during the 2013 to 2016 pilgrimages, and the autumn-winter respiratory disease burdens recorded among returning Iranian pilgrims in 2019. The findings regarding rhinovirus align with previous mass gathering surveillance, including 2019 Hajj data where rhinovirus was reported in 42.6 percent of symptomatic cases, and a 2017 study of Iranian pilgrims reporting a 20.19 percent prevalence. The researchers noted that while rhinovirus detection had dropped to 3.9 percent during the 2022 Hajj under rigorous pandemic-era non-pharmacological interventions, the higher frequencies observed in 2025 reflect post-pandemic transmission conditions. Endemic coronaviruses remained at modest levels across both cohorts (6 percent for 229E/NL63 and 2 percent for OC43/HKU1 in Arbaeen; 3.3 percent for OC43/HKU1 in Hajj), consistent with previous literature documenting peak circulation of endemic strains during winter and early spring rather than summer months. The study authors highlighted several methodological limitations that frame the interpretation of their results. The overall sample size of 110 participants was relatively small, constraining the broad generalizability of the findings across the millions of participating pilgrims. Furthermore, the researchers lacked access to granular clinical histories, symptom durations, and vaccination records for the tested individuals. Finally, the diagnostic multiplex kit employed was incapable of distinguishing between coronavirus OC43 and HKU1, or between coronavirus 229E and NL63, requiring their aggregation into grouped reporting categories. Despite these constraints, the authors concluded that these descriptive molecular data provide critical baseline insights for shaping future cross-border surveillance and public health preparedness strategies surrounding large-scale religious mass gatherings. According to the World Health Organization framework referenced in the study, mass gatherings are defined as events where large populations assemble in a designated location for an established purpose over a defined timeframe. During events such as the Hajj in Saudi Arabia and the Arbaeen walk, which commemorates the martyrdom of the third Shia Imam, Hossein ibn Ali, forty days after Ashura, transmission is facilitated by prolonged close contact and crowded environments. Physical fatigue among traveling pilgrims can also weaken immune defenses, leaving attendees susceptible to circulating respiratory pathogens. The researchers noted that prior Hajj surveillance indicated over one-third of pilgrims experience respiratory symptoms, with viral infections predominating among elderly attendees with chronic conditions. Similarly, research examining three hundred travelers during the 2023 Arbaeen pilgrimage documented flu-like illnesses among 53 percent of participants, while findings by Lami and colleagues highlighted cough in 25.6 percent and nasal discharge in 22.6 percent of pilgrims, emphasizing the role of hand hygiene facilities. The elevated proportion of coronavirus detections recorded among Arbaeen travelers also broadens observations from wider epidemiologic reviews. A systematic synthesis by Goumballa and colleagues documented SARS-CoV-2 infection rates spanning 1 to 15 percent during the 2021 and 2022 Hajj and Umrah pilgrimages, alongside an estimated 3 percent prevalence during the 2021 Arbaeen gathering. That analysis emphasized that cross-border viral transmission remains sensitive to host and home country transmission dynamics, local population crowding, circulating variant profiles, and underlying community immunity, warning that returning travelers could introduce viral lineages into their domestic settings. Meanwhile, the complete absence of MERS-CoV in the 2025 cohort corroborates multi-year surveillance conducted between 2013 and 2019 by Mercier, Alfelali, and Al-Tawfiq, which similarly identified no active MERS-CoV infections among returning Hajj participants. This continued negative finding contrasts with 2014 surveillance by Yavarian and colleagues that confirmed five cases in Iran, after which no further infections were identified in subsequent cohorts. Regarding endemic coronaviruses, earlier assessments demonstrate noticeable variance across settings; Barasheed and colleagues observed 2 percent OC43 and 229E positivity during the 2013 Hajj, whereas Hashem and colleagues reported 15.5 percent NL63 and 9.2 percent 229E. Additionally, Mercier and colleagues identified 12 percent 229E and 8.4 percent OC43, and Hoang and colleagues noted elevated 229E and OC43 circulation without SARS-CoV-2. Methodologically, the investigating laboratory validated all real-time PCR procedures using positive and negative no-template controls, and analyzed demographic and infection frequencies with SPSS version 22. The research, conducted by the National Influenza Center at Tehran University of Medical Sciences, analyzed 110 participants, with 60 from the Hajj and 50 from the Arbaeen walk. Rhinovirus was detected in 23.3% of Hajj participants and 36% of Arbaeen participants, while SARS-CoV-2 was found in 1.7% and 32% of these groups, respectively. The study attributed the difference in SARS-CoV-2 prevalence to variations in preventive protocols, crowd density, and local healthcare environments. It also noted that the overall viral positivity rate was higher among Arbaeen participants (78%) compared to Hajj participants (30%). The researchers emphasized methodological limitations, including the absence of vaccination records and differences in sampling procedures, which hinder direct comparisons of transmission risk between the two events. The findings align with previous studies on respiratory infections in mass gatherings, highlighting the role of seasonal dynamics and public health measures in shaping pathogen distribution.

news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Computational Study Identifies Distinct Structural and Epitope Patterns in Metapneumovirus Fusion Proteins by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Computational Study Identifies Distinct Structural and Epitope Patterns in Metapneumovirus Fusion Proteins Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A computational comparative investigation of the human metapneumovirus fusion protein across five viral subtypes has uncovered distinct structural profiles, physicochemical properties, and predicted antigenic patterns that distinguish genotype B from genotype A variants. Human metapneumovirus represents an enveloped, non-segmented, single-stranded negative-sense RNA pathogen within the Pneumoviridae family and Metapneumovirus genus, recognized as a leading cause of acute respiratory tract infections in humans, particularly presenting severe risks for the elderly and immunocompromised individuals. Because the viral fusion protein mediates host cell attachment, membrane fusion, and viral entry via Arg-Gly-Asp integrin interactions, it serves as the primary target for neutralizing antibody responses and candidate vaccine design, though no approved vaccine currently exists. To perform the comparative profiling, the study selected five representative reference GenBank accessions corresponding to genotypes A1, A2a, A2b, B1, and B2, specifically choosing accession records OL794389.1, PP086006.1, LC769208.1, OL794372.1, and OL794470.1. Each accession was chosen based on full-length sequence availability, unambiguous genotype annotation, absence of ambiguous amino acid residues, and frequent historical application in published literature to maintain analytical consistency. Sequence alignment across all five genotypes demonstrated that all examined fusion proteins share an identical length of 539 amino acids, encoded within viral genomes that range in length from 13,286 base pairs in subtype B2 to 13,440 base pairs in subtype A2b. Multiple sequence alignments and subsequent evolutionary modeling executed using MEGA X identified the Jones-Taylor-Thornton substitution model as the optimal fit for constructing a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree with 1,000 bootstrap replications, which was subsequently visualized using Figtree software. Phylogenetic reconstruction segregated the five fusion protein sequences into three primary clades, displaying a branching topology consistent with previous whole-genome phylogenetic analyses. Clade 1 incorporated the subtype A2a and A2b fusion proteins with a 65.7 percent bootstrap support value, while Clade 2 consisted exclusively of the subtype A1 fusion protein. Clade 3 clustered both subtype B1 and B2 fusion proteins together with 100 percent bootstrap confidence, reflecting the robust evolutionary cohesion characteristic of B genotypes relative to the more divergent A lineage. This structural tree topology mirrors previous whole-genome evaluations demonstrating that subtype B strains form significantly stronger clades with one another than do genotype A representatives, providing an evolutionary backdrop for the accompanying biochemical and structural variations observed across the two major lineages. Discover more Order DNA Kits Study Biology Study Chemistry Meet Dietitians Find Lung Care Analysis of physicochemical parameters using ProtParam revealed distinct markers separating genotype B from genotype A fusion proteins, notably in their calculated theoretical isoelectric points, atomic compositions, and aliphatic indices. Both subtype B1 and B2 proteins exhibited an identical theoretical isoelectric point of 6.94, contrasting with the more basic isoelectric points observed across the A genotypes, which measured 8.10 for A1, 8.27 for A2a, and 7.84 for A2b. Elemental calculations also revealed that both subtype B proteins possess exactly 24 sulfur atoms, compared to 23 sulfur atoms in each of the three genotype A proteins, alongside close molecular weights ranging between 58,443.19 Daltons for B2 and 58,602.33 Daltons for A2b. Thermodynamic and hydropathic evaluations indicated differences in thermal stability and hydrophobicity between the major subtype groupings. While the instability index across all five proteins fell below the threshold value of 40—ranging from 35.20 in subtype A1 to 36.71 in subtype B1—confirming that all examined structures are stable in silico, the aliphatic index was consistently higher in the B genotypes. Subtype B1 and B2 recorded aliphatic indices of 99.48 and 98.94 respectively, whereas all genotype A proteins registered values below 98.50, indicating greater relative thermal stability for the B genotype proteins. Similarly, the grand average of hydropathicity scores were elevated in subtype B1 at 0.045 and B2 at 0.044 compared to 0.028 in A1, 0.024 in A2a, and 0.027 in A2b, reflecting a greater overall nonpolar hydrophobic character that may influence protein folding, stability, and membrane-fusion activity. Discover more Check Symptoms Read Med Journals Browse Art Prints Despite differences in molecular weight and aliphatic character, several structural parameters remained invariant across all five viral subtypes. The estimated protein half-life in silico remained constant at 30 hours in mammalian reticulocytes in vitro, exceeding 20 hours in yeast in vivo, and exceeding 10 hours in Escherichia coli in vivo, assuming methionine at the amino terminus. Detailed composition checks confirmed that the quantities of cysteine, tryptophan, histidine, and leucine residues were strictly conserved across all five proteins. In contrast, the counts of methionine, proline, isoleucine, and serine were uniquely conserved within subtype B fusion proteins, presenting a preliminary computational fingerprint to distinguish between subtypes A and B before proceeding to functional validation. Post-translational modification profiling using NetPhos, NetNGlyc, NetCGlyc, and YinOYang demonstrated both conserved and subtype-specific enzymatic targeting sites. Across all examined variants, the predicted counts of tyrosine phosphorylation sites, potential N-type glycosylation sites, and potential C-mannosylation sites remained identical at 6, 3, and 4 sites, respectively. However, predicted serine phosphorylation varied from 32 sites in A2b and B2 to 35 sites in A1, while threonine phosphorylation sites ranged between 15 sites in A1 and 17 sites in A2a and B2. Potential O-type glycosylation sites spanned between 82 sites in A2a, A2b, and B1 to 83 sites in A1 and B2. In viral biology, phosphorylation influences cellular signaling and protein viability, whereas glycosylation patterns orchestrate viral binding, host membrane entry, structural stability, and antibody neutralization shielding. Antigenic profiling performed with SVMTriP using a 0.5 threshold score and cross-referenced against the Immune Epitope Database revealed substantial divergence in predicted antigenic density between the lineages. Subtype B1 and B2 fusion proteins each yielded 10 predicted antigenic epitopes, whereas subtype A1 and A2a yielded only 6, and subtype A2b yielded 7. Across all genotypes, only three predicted epitope sequences were universally shared between both genotype groups, indicating that the two groups may maintain divergent mechanisms for navigating host immune pressure. High-scoring epitope clusters mapped predominantly to antigenic sites III and IV of the fusion protein, which represent canonical targets for neutralizing human antibodies such as MPV364, MPE8, and DS7, while additional predicted epitopes localized to structural interfaces adjacent to sites II and V. Three-dimensional macromolecular modeling via Phyre2 in intensive mode, utilizing high-confidence paramyxovirus fusion protein structural templates exceeding 99 percent template coverage and 95 percent confidence, produced largely superimposable ectodomain backbones across all genotypes. The closest Protein Data Bank match for all predicted structures was identified as chain A of entry C5wb0, displaying 100 percent model confidence alongside 99 percent sequence identity for genotype A models and 95 to 96 percent identity for genotype B models. Ramachandran plot validation confirmed favorable stereochemical parameters across all models, with 94.98 percent of residues located within favored regions, 2.28 percent within allowed regions, and 2.74 percent within disallowed regions, the latter predominantly comprising glycine residues. The NCBI Conserved Domain Database identified the conserved functional fusion glycoprotein F0 domain spanning residues 21 through 495, while cellular localization algorithms predicted distribution in both the host cell membrane and endoplasmic reticulum. Transmembrane topology assessments conducted with TMHMM version 2.0, SOSUI, and Phobius revealed structural variation in the predicted number of transmembrane helices, identifying three domains in subtypes A1, A2a, and B2, but only two in subtypes A2b and B1. All proteins contained an identical 18-amino-acid signal peptide from residues 1 to 18, a first transmembrane domain from residues 103 to 125, and a third domain from residues 491 to 513, while transmembrane domain 2 at residues 256 to 278 was absent in A2b and B1. The study author emphasized that these bioinformatic findings are strictly exploratory and hypothesis-generating, having been derived from five single-accession representatives. Consequently, all identified physicochemical discriminators, predicted epitopes, and topological variations represent provisional computational observations that require rigorous in vitro and in vivo experimental validation across wider sample cohorts before being applied to human clinical interventions or definitive vaccine formulations. analysis.brief_en: A computational study published on November 23, 2026, by Bioengineer.org analyzed the fusion proteins of human metapneumovirus (hMPV) across five subtypes: A1, A2a, A2b, B1, and B2. The research identified distinct structural and epitope patterns, particularly separating genotype B from genotype A variants. The study found that all five fusion proteins share an identical length of 539 amino acids, but they differ in isoelectric points, sulfur atom counts, molecular weights, and antigenic epitopes. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the subtypes into three clades, with genotype B showing stronger cohesion. The study also revealed differences in thermal stability and hydrophobicity between the subtypes. These findings provide insights into the molecular and immunological characteristics of hMPV, which may inform future vaccine development. news.content: Skip to main content Search Products Community Markets Brokers More EN Black FridayUp to 80% OFF News /MarketBeat /Sanofi Maps Vaccine Pipeline With Flu-COVID and Pneumococcal Trial Results Ahead Sanofi Maps Vaccine Pipeline With Flu-COVID and Pneumococcal Trial Results Ahead 3 min read SNY+4.80%SAN+4.89% Giants Costco, Sanofi, and SAP Raise Dividends by Over 10% Sanofi SNY is advancing a slate of vaccine candidates targeting respiratory infections, pneumococcal disease and acne, with several clinical readouts expected over the next 18 months, according to its head of vaccines research and development. Jean-François Toussaint said the company recently began a phase III immunogenicity study of a combined flu and COVID-19 vaccine and expects results within that period. Sanofi also expects results from pediatric phase III trials of its 21-component pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in 2027. The programs are part of a vaccine pipeline that Toussaint said has been prioritized over several years. He said vaccines remain an important growth driver under CEO Belén Garijo, alongside immunology and inflammation and rare diseases. Respiratory and pneumococcal programs Toussaint described the flu-COVID combination as a potential growth driver, combining Sanofi’s flu vaccine with a COVID vaccine from Novavax. He said the company is also developing a combined vaccine for respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, and human metapneumovirus, or hMPV. Sanofi has two RSV-hMPV candidates: one based on messenger RNA and another acquired through Vicebio. Toussaint said the Vicebio candidate is designed to be stored as a liquid in a prefilled syringe in a refrigerator, and the company expects it to allow a boosted immune response. He cautioned that Sanofi does not yet have all the data needed to decide which approach is best. The company has started a phase IIb study of an RSV-hMPV candidate to monitor efficacy and assess a suitable endpoint for hMPV before a potentially expensive phase III trial. Toussaint said he hopes to have data in about 18 months, though he was unsure whether the company would share the results publicly. For its pneumococcal candidate, known as PCV21, Sanofi has six phase III trials underway in children. Toussaint said the company is not counting on a preferential recommendation over existing vaccines based on the number of components alone. Instead, he pointed to Sanofi’s pediatric vaccine portfolio and commercial scale as potential advantages in winning market share if the candidate succeeds. Acne vaccine and broader research Sanofi has expanded a phase II trial of its acne vaccine candidate to 800 volunteers from an initial 200. Toussaint said the larger study should provide a more robust indication of whether the vaccine works and whether it benefits particular patient groups. He pointed to 2028 for results. The candidate aims to neutralize bacteria and the toxin they produce to limit inflammation, Toussaint said. Beyond acne, he said a positive result could provide proof of concept for developing vaccines against other pathogens that trigger inflammation. Sanofi also obtained an experimental shingles vaccine through its Dynavax deal. Toussaint said the candidate has produced good data in younger adults, but the company needs to see results in older adults before determining its path forward. Pipeline priorities and partnerships Toussaint said Sanofi previously discontinued an mRNA flu vaccine program despite results comparable to competitors because the company did not believe the technology would make a difference in that market. Vaccine pipeline prioritization remains an ongoing process, he said. Asked about cancer vaccines following melanoma data from Moderna, Toussaint said Sanofi has an mRNA platform that could potentially be used in the field, but that he was not convinced the company would pursue cancer vaccines itself. He said providing access to the platform to another developer could be an option. Toussaint also discussed Beyfortus, the RSV antibody product Sanofi co-developed with AstraZeneca. He said both maternal immunization and monoclonal antibodies can reduce hospitalization risk, but argued that the antibody approach offers longer-lasting protection and more flexibility in timing administration for infants. About Sanofi SNY Sanofi is a France-based global biopharmaceutical company that researches, develops, manufactures and markets medicines and vaccines. Its work spans areas including immunology, oncology, rare diseases and neurology, as well as preventive vaccines. The company's portfolio includes Dupixent, an immunology medicine developed with Regeneron, and vaccines for diseases such as influenza and meningitis. Sanofi serves patients and healthcare providers in markets around the world. Sanofi traces its origins to a company established in France in 1973. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Viral Co-Detection Associated With Longer Hospital Stays in Infants With RSV by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Viral Co-Detection Associated With Longer Hospital Stays in Infants With RSV Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Infants under one year old diagnosed with lower respiratory tract infections attributed to respiratory syncytial virus experienced longer hospital stays when co-infected with additional viruses, according to a multicenter study in Japan. Although the presence of multiple viral pathogens was associated with a longer hospital stay, it was not significantly associated with increased respiratory-support requirements or greater oxygen needs. The clinical investigation evaluated the epidemiological patterns and clinical impacts of co-detection before the introduction of new preventative prophylactic drugs for respiratory syncytial virus. Respiratory syncytial virus is recognized as a major cause of lower respiratory tract infections in infants, alongside various other respiratory viruses. Prior to this investigation, researchers noted that medical literature lacked clear conclusions regarding how frequently co-detection occurs in pediatric patients with respiratory syncytial virus. In addition, existing studies had not established which microorganisms tend to overlap with the virus or whether such simultaneous infections contribute to enhanced clinical severity in affected infants. To address these questions, investigators conducted pathogenic microbial analyses across medical institutions in Chiba City and Ichihara City, Japan. The study evaluated pediatric cases between 2021 and 2023, enrolling infants under 12 months of age who presented with suspected respiratory syncytial virus lower respiratory tract infections. Medical staff administered rapid antigen testing to each infant as part of their diagnostic evaluation for suspected illness. Discover more Engineering Job Board Research Paper Access Learn Engineering Track Biotech Tour Colleges Following the initial evaluations, researchers performed multiplex polymerase chain reaction panel testing using residual samples obtained from the rapid antigen tests. The research team documented the specific microorganisms detected across the cohort and evaluated key patient demographics and clinical outcomes. Specifically, investigators examined patient age, hospitalization rates, length of hospital stay, and the need for respiratory support, comparing infants in whom the virus was detected alone against cases where other pathogens were detected simultaneously. The cross-sectional investigation enrolled a total of 492 infants presenting with lower respiratory tract infections. Among this cohort, 252 infants, representing 51.2 percent of participants, tested positive for respiratory syncytial virus. Within this group, researchers identified two or more viruses in 91 infants, establishing a viral co-detection rate of 36.1 percent. In comparison, one or more viruses were detected in 207 of the 240 infants who tested negative for respiratory syncytial virus, reflecting a detection rate of 86.3 percent. Pathogen analysis demonstrated distinct epidemiological characteristics among detected microorganisms over the study period. Rhinovirus/enterovirus and adenovirus were identified consistently throughout the year, whereas parainfluenza virus 3 exhibited a distinct seasonal peak. The authors observed that the detection of several other respiratory viruses was significantly less common in infants testing positive for respiratory syncytial virus than in negative infants. Furthermore, viral co-detection became more frequent with increasing age among infants younger than 12 months. In terms of clinical severity, the presence of multiple viral pathogens was linked to an extended hospital stay, yet it showed no significant association with requirements for respiratory support. However, specific viral infections presented notable clinical risks within certain age brackets. Human metapneumovirus was commonly detected among infants under six months of age, and nearly half of these patients required the administration of oxygen therapy. Discover more Study Biology Study Chemistry Read Health Guides Lab Equipment Sales Donate to Research The study concluded that among infants younger than one year, viral co-detection occurs with increasing frequency as age advances. While harboring multiple pathogens did not translate into greater oxygen requirements or elevated respiratory support, it was associated with extended hospital stays for infants treated for respiratory syncytial virus lower respiratory tract infections. These clinical findings provide baseline epidemiological data established prior to the introduction of new prophylactic drugs in Japan. The research team documented the specific microorganisms detected across the cohort and evaluated key patient demographics and clinical outcomes. Specifically, investigators examined patient age, hospitalization rates, length of hospital stay, and the need for respiratory support, comparing infants in whom the virus was detected alone against cases where other pathogens were detected simultaneously. The cross-sectional investigation enrolled a total of 492 infants presenting with lower respiratory tract infections. Among this cohort, 252 infants, representing 51.2 percent of participants, tested positive for respiratory syncytial virus. Within this group, researchers identified two or more viruses in 91 infants, establishing a viral co-detection rate of 36.1 percent. In comparison, one or more viruses were detected in 207 of the 240 infants who tested negative for respiratory syncytial virus, reflecting a detection rate of 86.3 percent. Pathogen analysis demonstrated distinct epidemiological characteristics among detected microorganisms over the study period. Rhinovirus/enterovirus and adenovirus were identified consistently throughout the year, whereas parainfluenza virus 3 exhibited a distinct seasonal peak. The authors observed that the detection of several other respiratory viruses was significantly less common in infants testing positive for respiratory syncytial virus than in negative infants. Furthermore, viral co-detection became more frequent with increasing age among infants younger than 12 months. In terms of clinical severity, the presence of multiple viral pathogens was linked to an extended hospital stay, yet it showed no significant association with requirements for respiratory support. However, specific viral infections presented notable clinical risks within certain age brackets. Human metapneumovirus was commonly detected among infants under six months of age, and nearly half of these patients required the administration of oxygen therapy. While harboring multiple pathogens did not translate into greater oxygen requirements or elevated respiratory support, it was associated with extended hospital stays for infants treated for respiratory syncytial virus lower respiratory tract infections. These clinical findings provide baseline epidemiological data established prior to the introduction of new prophylactic drugs in Japan. news.content: WGNO Louisiana has highest rate of respiratory infections; holidays could make things worse Hunter Trombetta 4 hours ago NEW ORLEANS (WGNO) — Louisiana is the number one state in the country when it comes to reported respiratory illnesses, according to the CDC. “Unfortunately, we do have that distinction. And it’s not just the influenza. We’re dealing with higher rates of flu, and higher rates of lots of other bugs,” says Dr. Craig Naccari, a primary care physician with LCMC Health. “A lot of Covid, rhinovirus, I’ve seen some human metapneumovirus. So, a lot of respiratory infections going around all around.” Naccari says those cases are likely to get even more common as friends and family get together for the holidays. “These things will trickle in, and then holiday will hit, and it will explode. So, every person who is infected infects 10 more people, and then rapidly the hospitals fill up with sick people,” says Naccari. “We’re hoping that’s not going to happen after this holiday week, but that is kind of the expectation.” He says a good first line of defense is the flu shot, but even that is not a guarantee. “It’s not the best shot in the world. On a good year it’s around 50% effective,” says Naccari. “It can vary a little bit, but it is effective for a lot of people, and if it reduces your chance by about 50%, that’s pretty darn good.” He says the best thing to do is to keep an eye out for symptoms and don’t spoil someone else’s holidays by getting them sick. “If you get sort of a light sniffle, don’t assume it’s allergies or something like that, because you might be spreading around a lot of illness to potentially susceptible people. So that’s kind of a low bar to go talk to a doctor, and get yourself checked out,” says Naccari. “And then if you’re sick, stay home. Don’t spread it around. Just be considerate to your fellow man.” Stay up to date with the latest news, weather and sports by downloading the WGNO app on the Apple or Google Play stores and by subscribing to the WGNO newsletter. news.source_body_en: Louisiana is reported to have the highest rate of respiratory infections in the country, according to the CDC, as highlighted by WGNO. The situation is expected to worsen during the holiday season due to increased social interactions, which could lead to a surge in cases. Dr. Craig Naccari, a primary care physician with LCMC Health, notes that the current rates include higher occurrences of flu and human metapneumovirus (hMPV), among other respiratory pathogens. He warns that each infected person can infect up to 10 others, potentially overwhelming hospitals. While the flu shot is recommended as a first line of defense, it is noted to be only about 50% effective. Naccari advises individuals to monitor symptoms and avoid spreading illness by staying home if they are unwell. The report is based on current data and projections, with no confirmed case or death counts provided.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hospitalized Pediatric Human Metapneumovirus Infections Shifted Toward Younger Infants in Taiwan by November 25, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Hospitalized Pediatric Human Metapneumovirus Infections Shifted Toward Younger Infants in Taiwan Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A three-year multicenter observational cohort investigation conducted across three hospitals in Taiwan has tracked the epidemiological patterns, clinical manifestations, and genomic features of human metapneumovirus among hospitalized pediatric patients following post-pandemic viral resurgence. Between January 2023 and December 2025, investigators systematically evaluated acute respiratory tract infections in children under eighteen years of age, identifying human metapneumovirus in nearly twelve percent of systematically screened hospital admissions. The research uncovered a notable temporal transition in the age distribution of affected children, marked by a progressive shift from older children toward younger infants over the consecutive surveillance years. The study also characterized co-circulating viral lineages, identified distinct amino acid substitutions within the viral fusion protein in emerging strains, and detailed clinical outcomes across varying levels of hospital care, providing comprehensive epidemiological evidence on pediatric human metapneumovirus activity during the post-pandemic recovery era. Human metapneumovirus was initially identified in 2001 as a widespread respiratory pathogen belonging to the Pneumoviridae family, sharing genetic relationships with respiratory syncytial virus. Worldwide pooled prevalence estimates indicate that the virus accounts for approximately 5.3 percent of respiratory tract infections across all age brackets, reaching its highest documented prevalence of 6.7 percent among children younger than five years and falling to 2.5 percent among adults. The viral genome spans roughly 13,300 base pairs encoding eight genes, with the fusion protein serving as the primary neutralizing antibody target and both the fusion and attachment glycoprotein genes utilized for molecular classification. The pathogen divides into two major genotypes, designated A and B, comprising four circulating sublineages termed A1, A2, B1, and B2. Following extensive disruptions to typical viral seasonality during the COVID-19 pandemic, widespread post-pandemic resurgences were recorded internationally, yet comprehensive clinical and molecular data within Taiwanese healthcare settings remained sparse. To evaluate these dynamics, researchers implemented a hybrid retrospective and prospective cohort protocol collaborating between the National Taiwan University Children’s Hospital, an academic tertiary medical center situated in northern Taiwan, and the Show Chwan Healthcare System, encompassing two community hospitals located in Changhua County within central Taiwan. The investigation enrolled hospitalized children younger than eighteen years diagnosed with acute respiratory illness who underwent molecular testing with either the BioFire FilmArray Respiratory Panel 2.1 or the Pneumonia Panel. Period 1 spanned January 2023 through June 2024 as a retrospective electronic medical record review, while Period 2 operated prospectively from July 2024 through December 2025, gathering nasopharyngeal swabs and structured clinical records after obtaining written informed parental consent. Across the entire cohort, lower respiratory tract illness was classified by attending physicians into bronchitis, bronchiolitis, bronchopneumonia, or pneumonia, while dyspnea was documented by observable nasal flaring or intercostal and subcostal retractions. Across the thirty-six months of hospital surveillance, clinical teams performed molecular screening panels on 3310 hospitalized pediatric admissions presenting with acute respiratory conditions, identifying at least one causative respiratory pathogen in 2652 individuals, representing 80.1 percent of all screened tests. Rhinovirus or enterovirus appeared as the most prevalent detected agent at 38.2 percent, followed in frequency by respiratory syncytial virus at 15.2 percent, parainfluenza viruses at 14.8 percent, adenovirus at 14.4 percent, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae at 12.3 percent. Human metapneumovirus ranked as the sixth most frequent pathogen, detected in 390 patients, or 11.8 percent of tested cases, including 233 detections during the retrospective phase and 157 during the prospective phase. Following the exclusion of forty-eight prospective cases lacking parental consent, the research team analyzed detailed medical, laboratory, and therapeutic records for 342 confirmed pediatric inpatients across the participating institutions. The cohort of 342 hospitalized children exhibited a median age of 2.77 years with an interquartile range from 1.30 to 4.64 years, and male patients comprised 51.2 percent of the population. Lower respiratory tract involvement dominated clinical admissions, documented in 93.6 percent of cases, whereas upper respiratory tract diagnoses accounted for only 6.4 percent. Chronic underlying medical conditions were present in 41.5 percent of the overall cohort, though such comorbidities appeared with significantly greater frequency among children treated at the tertiary children’s hospital than in the community hospital system, recording 61.7 percent versus 19.1 percent. The specific pre-existing diagnoses included low birth weight in 15.2 percent, prematurity in 13.7 percent, asthma in 8.8 percent, congenital heart disease in 5.3 percent, chronic neurological disorders in 4.1 percent, genetic or chromosomal disorders in 1.5 percent, active malignancy in 1.2 percent, and diagnosed immunodeficiency in 0.9 percent. Clinical presentations were characterized by fever in 98.2 percent of children, lasting for an overall median duration of 4 days, alongside cough in 95.0 percent, audible wheezing in 34.2 percent, shortness of breath or dyspnea in 33.3 percent, and visible chest retractions in 20.8 percent. Laboratory evaluations demonstrated a median white blood cell count of 8.65 thousand cells per microliter and a median neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio of 1.51 across the study sites. Viral co-infections were confirmed in 43.9 percent of the children, with rhinovirus detected in 24.9 percent, parainfluenza in 9.2 percent, and adenovirus in 8.7 percent. Respiratory bacterial cultures were obtained for 179 children, yielding positive pathogenic cultures in 46.4 percent of tested individuals, predominantly Haemophilus influenzae at 14.6 percent and Moraxella catarrhalis at 14.3 percent, while Streptococcus pneumoniae was confirmed in only 4.4 percent. Radiographic abnormalities, defined as pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrates, were noted in 30.8 percent of evaluated chest radiographs. Hospital management entailed a median inpatient duration of 6 days, with 17.1 percent of evaluated patients requiring pediatric intensive care unit admission and staying an intensive care median of 5 days. Prescribed clinical therapies included systemic or inhaled antibiotics in 66.4 percent of children, bronchodilators in 57.9 percent, and systemic corticosteroid treatments in 17.5 percent, without any fatal outcomes recorded in the cohort. Overall, 39.8 percent of inpatients required some form of respiratory support, encompassing supplemental oxygen in 97 children and advanced respiratory support modalities in 39 cases. Advanced modalities comprised high-flow nasal cannula in 27 individuals, bilevel positive airway pressure in 7 patients, and invasive mechanical ventilation in 5 children. Multivariable regression demonstrated that the need for advanced respiratory support was independently associated with pre-existing neurological disorders, with an adjusted odds ratio of 5.76, and pulmonary consolidation or patchy infiltrations on radiographs, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.44. Epidemiological surveillance identified an annual seasonal recurrence that was remarkably consistent across all three monitored years, marked by an expansion of viral activity commencing in February, a defined peak in April, and declining detection by July. Simultaneously, analysis of patient demographics demonstrated a progressive decline in the median age of hospitalized children from 3.45 years in 2023 to 3.06 years in 2024, falling to 2.12 years by 2025. Statistical trend testing confirmed that the proportion of hospitalized infants aged zero to one year increased significantly over the three years, while the proportion of affected children older than five years dropped significantly. The authors noted that older children accounted for an elevated share of hospitalizations during the initial 2023 resurgence wave before hospital admissions reverted toward the customary younger pediatric demographic, aligning with international observations documented in Japan and other jurisdictions following post-pandemic re-emergence. Molecular sequencing and phylogenetic analysis of prospective specimens successfully characterized the fusion gene of 124 human metapneumovirus isolates, identifying genotype A in 85 specimens, representing 68.5 percent, and genotype B in 39 specimens, representing 31.5 percent. Phylogenetic trees constructed using maximum-likelihood methods on 78 complete fusion gene coding sequences demonstrated that all four global sublineages co-circulated in Taiwan, with sublineage A2.2.2 constituting the predominant lineage. Furthermore, circulating genotype B2 viruses isolated during the 2025 season were marked by two specific amino acid substitutions in the fusion protein, designated L36H and K179R, which mirrored emerging variant strains identified in regional outbreaks within mainland China during the corresponding 2024 to 2025 period. Comparative clinical analyses between genotype A and genotype B revealed broadly similar symptomatology, diagnoses, and interventions, although children with genotype B presented with a higher frequency of neurological disorders and higher median leukocyte counts. The study authors highlighted several methodological limitations that contextualize their observational conclusions, including the relatively modest number of successfully sequenced viral amplicons and the exclusive analysis of the fusion gene coding region. Because the viral attachment glycoprotein gene was not sequenced, the researchers could not verify whether the predominant A2.2.2 strains harbored the 111-nucleotide or 180-nucleotide gene duplications described in other international cohorts. Additionally, clinical specimens were unavailable for sequencing from the 2023 to 2024 period, preventing uninterrupted continuous molecular tracking across the complete three-year span. The investigators also emphasized that differences in data collection between the retrospective and prospective study phases, potential selection bias from consent requirements, single-country geographic scope, and lack of comparative pathogen controls warrant cautious interpretation of the observed age shifts, underscoring the necessity for sustained multicenter molecular surveillance to monitor ongoing viral evolution and transmission.
