supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, November 26, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Computational Study Identifies Candidate Small Molecules Targeting Human Metapneumovirus Nucleocapsid by November 24, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Computational Study Identifies Candidate Small Molecules Targeting Human Metapneumovirus Nucleocapsid Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A computational drug discovery investigation has identified three candidate small-molecule inhibitors that demonstrate favorable binding affinity, structural stability, and drug-like properties against the nucleocapsid protein of human metapneumovirus. Human metapneumovirus, first isolated in 2001 within the family Paramyxoviridae, represents a leading cause of acute respiratory tract infections across all demographics, frequently resulting in severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia requiring hospitalization among pediatric, elderly, and immunocompromised populations. While seasonal outbreaks circulate globally and seroprevalence surveys indicate widespread infection by age five, host immunity remains incomplete, permitting lifelong reinfections transmitted via direct contact, respiratory droplets, and contaminated fomites. Despite this sustained morbidity and documented mortality risks during viral coinfection, there are currently no approved antiviral therapies or protective vaccines directed against the pathogen. Broad-spectrum antiviral treatments such as ribavirin have offered limited clinical efficacy, while monoclonal antibodies directed against the surface fusion protein encounter substantial production costs and sequence variability, accentuating the urgent requirement for targeted small-molecule therapeutics. To bypass the complications of antigenic drift observed in viral surface glycoproteins, researchers focused on the nucleocapsid protein, an indispensable structural component of human metapneumovirus. The single-stranded negative-sense RNA viral genome encodes nine proteins, including structural and nonstructural elements such as the fusion protein, attachment glycoprotein, small hydrophobic protein, matrix protein, large RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, phosphoprotein, and two nonstructural factors. The nucleocapsid protein plays a foundational role in safeguarding viral genetic material by encasing genomic RNA, preventing host immune recognition, and forming an active ribonucleoprotein replication complex alongside the viral phosphoprotein cofactor and the large polymerase enzyme. Because the nucleocapsid sequence is highly conserved across strains and serves an obligatory mechanical function in genomic encapsidation and transcriptional elongation, it represents an especially attractive antiviral target, as disruption of its binding interactions could suppress viral propagation and diminish overall clinical disease severity. The investigative team established a structured computational pipeline that integrated structure-based virtual screening, secondary redocking, continuous five-hundred-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations, free energy calculations, and absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion predictions. Structural modeling was anchored to the high-resolution crystal structure of the monomeric, RNA-free human metapneumovirus nucleocapsid protein bound to its phosphoprotein cofactor, cataloged under Protein Data Bank identifier 5FVD at a resolution of 1.86 angstroms. Preparation of the macromolecule was executed using the DockPrep utility within UCSF Chimera, wherein crystallographic water molecules were cleared, polar hydrogens were added, protonation states of active-site residues were inspected, and energetic minimization was conducted to relieve steric clashes. Binding cavity coordinates were computed using the CASTp server, prioritizing the largest predicted pocket which incorporates functional amino acid residues such as leucine 167, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, and methionine 337 that participate directly in RNA association and nucleoprotein oligomerization. Virtual screening commenced across the MTiOpenScreen academic platform, evaluating fifteen hundred pre-filtered drug-like molecules from the diverse-lib library to identify chemical scaffolds with high docking affinity and adherence to Lipinski rules. The screening scores across the library spanned an energetic spectrum from minus 10.7 to positive 8.3 kilocalories per mole. From this initial assessment, the three top-ranked candidate structures were shortlisted for secondary redocking using AutoDock Vina in UCSF Chimera alongside Gamma-Fagarine, a compound selected as a comparative reference standard due to its established antiviral relevance and baseline interaction stability within the target pocket. The three candidate compounds—designated by identifiers 24,330,502, 24,292,974, and 17,515,455—exhibited primary virtual screening scores of minus 10.7, minus 10.3, and minus 10.3 kilocalories per mole, substantially surpassing the reference molecule. Secondary redocking analyses validated the docking consistency of the shortlisted molecules, yielding binding energies of minus 10.2 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,330,502, minus 10.3 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,292,974, and minus 9.6 kilocalories per mole for compound 17,515,455. In contrast, Gamma-Fagarine produced a noticeably weaker redocking score of minus 6.3 kilocalories per mole, suggesting a diminished capacity for binding site occupancy. Chemically, compound 24,330,502 corresponds to PubChem identifier 1111158, designated systematically as 3,4-dihydroisoquinolin-2(1H)-yl[5-phenyl-7-(trifluoromethyl)pyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-3-yl]methanone. Compound 24,292,974 corresponds to PubChem identifier 4292500, chemically named N-(2-(4-fluorophenyl)-4,6-dihydro-2H-thieno[3,4-c]pyrazol-3-yl)-2-oxo-2H-chromene-3-carboxamide, while compound 17,515,455 corresponds to PubChem identifier 7125864, identified as 4-benzyl-1-(4-fluorophenyl)-[1,2,4]triazolo[4,3-a]quinazolin-5(4H)-one. The reference standard Gamma-Fagarine is recorded under PubChem identifier 107936. Detailed intermolecular contact mapping carried out with the Desmond and Maestro visualization modules demonstrated intricate noncovalent interaction networks that anchored the candidate ligands within the nucleocapsid binding groove. Compound 24,330,502 established an extensive hydrophobic network involving leucine 167, isoleucine 176, valine 178, alanine 254, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, isoleucine 335, and methionine 337, complemented by prominent pi-pi stacking interactions with tryptophan 261. Compound 24,292,974 developed direct hydrogen bonds with threonine 170 and serine 174, while also engaging hydrophobic contacts with leucine 167, isoleucine 176, valine 178, alanine 254, tryptophan 261, isoleucine 334, and isoleucine 335, alongside dual pi-pi stacking and cation-pi interactions involving arginine 186 and tryptophan 261. Compound 17,515,455 anchored through a hydrogen bond with threonine 257, an extensive hydrophobic assembly with residues including leucine 167, alanine 254, and methionine 337, and both pi-pi stacking and cation-pi associations with arginine 186 and tryptophan 261. By comparison, Gamma-Fagarine established hydrogen bonds with serine 174, threonine 257, and arginine 260, but engaged fewer hydrophobic contacts and lacked pi-pi stacking altogether. To evaluate the conformational behavior and kinetic stability of the complexes under simulated physiological conditions, unconstrained five-hundred-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations were conducted using Desmond and Maestro with the OPLS-2005 force field. Each solvated system was enclosed in an orthorhombic periodic boundary box of TIP3P water molecules with ten angstroms of buffer clearance, neutralized through sodium and chloride counter-ions, and adjusted to 0.15 molar sodium chloride. Systems underwent two-stage energy minimization followed by consecutive NVT equilibration at 300 Kelvin via Berendsen thermostats and NPT equilibration at one atmosphere utilizing Nosé-Hoover thermostats and Martyna-Tobias-Klein barostats. Particle mesh Ewald summations governed electrostatic forces, with van der Waals cutoffs established at ten angstroms, recording trajectories every ten picoseconds over the five-hundred-nanosecond production phase. Root mean square deviation trajectories confirmed that the top candidate complexes attained structural equilibrium across the simulation timeframe. The complex formed by compound 24,330,502 demonstrated exceptional stability, maintaining low protein and ligand root mean square deviation values below four angstroms with minimal fluctuations throughout the trajectory. Compound 24,292,974 displayed a steady protein backbone but exhibited ligand deviations that reached up to twelve angstroms, indicating dynamic conformational adjustments within the cavity. Compound 17,515,455 maintained steady coordinates before undergoing a minor deviation shift near four hundred nanoseconds consistent with localized ligand repositioning. Conversely, the Gamma-Fagarine complex exhibited profound instability, with ligand deviations surpassing thirty angstroms, reflecting weak target retention and progressive dissociation from the binding pocket. Complementary root mean square fluctuation analyses of protein residues and ligand coordinates affirmed that critical amino acids forming the binding pocket experienced minimal atomic deviation, although terminal protein segments exhibited expected flexibility. Ligand fluctuation measurements showed that compound 24,330,502 experienced the lowest internal fluctuation, confirming a rigid, well-accommodated binding posture. While compound 24,292,974 and compound 17,515,455 displayed moderate flexibility, the reference standard Gamma-Fagarine generated extreme fluctuations ranging between twelve and fifteen angstroms. Principal component analysis substantiated these dynamics across the first two eigenvectors, which accounted for substantial variance proportions. Projections for compound 24,330,502, whose first two principal components captured 54.1 percent and 15.1 percent of variance respectively, formed compact, well-defined clusters indicative of homogenous structural sampling. In contrast, Gamma-Fagarine generated widely dispersed projections spanning 56.0 percent and 18.2 percent of variance, denoting extensive structural transitions and lack of stable complexation. Thermodynamic stability was further interrogated through free energy landscape construction and structural superimposition of representative low-energy conformations against initial docked coordinates. Free energy landscape projections generated via the Geo-Measures plugin revealed that compound 24,330,502 resided within a deep, singular, concentrated energy basin, reflecting a stable state. Compounds 24,292,974 and 17,515,455 navigated multiple shallow energy minima representing permissible conformational flexibility, whereas Gamma-Fagarine yielded fragmented, shallow basins characteristic of unstable binding. Superimposition of the lowest-energy conformations extracted from simulation trajectories demonstrated minimal structural drift from original docking coordinates, yielding root mean square deviations of 1.928 angstroms for compound 24,330,502, 1.722 angstroms for compound 24,292,974, and 2.029 angstroms for compound 17,515,455, compared with 1.855 angstroms for Gamma-Fagarine. End-point binding free energy calculations performed using the Prime MM/GBSA method over the final fifty nanoseconds of trajectory confirmed robust thermodynamic affinities for the candidate molecules. Compound 17,515,455 achieved the most favorable net binding free energy of minus 74.57 plus or minus 7.81 kilocalories per mole, followed by compound 24,330,502 at minus 68.83 plus or minus 4.47 kilocalories per mole, and compound 24,292,974 at minus 45.75 plus or minus 3.61 kilocalories per mole. In stark contrast, Gamma-Fagarine yielded a significantly weaker binding free energy of minus 24.89 plus or minus 2.28 kilocalories per mole. Energetic decomposition highlighted that nonpolar forces drove complexation, with van der Waals contributions reaching minus 54.52 kilocalories per mole for compound 17,515,455 and minus 53.73 kilocalories per mole for compound 24,330,502. These were reinforced by favorable lipophilic free energies of minus 26.79 plus or minus 1.56 and minus 21.01 plus or minus 1.09 kilocalories per mole, alongside favorable electrostatic contributions for compounds 24,330,502 and 17,515,455. Pharmacokinetic and physicochemical evaluations using SwissADME revealed generally favorable drug-likeness profiles alongside specific liabilities that direct future lead optimization. All three candidate compounds demonstrated high predicted gastrointestinal absorption, absence of pan-assay interference compounds structural alerts, and identical bioavailability scores of 0.55. Compounds 24,330,502 and 24,292,974 satisfied Lipinski rule-of-five criteria with zero violations, while compound 17,515,455 exhibited a single violation. Synthetic accessibility scores ranged favorably from 2.90 to 3.57. However, the profiling flagged several optimization requirements: compounds 24,330,502 and 17,515,455 showed predicted blood-brain barrier permeability, multiple cytochrome P450 isoenzyme inhibition liabilities across CYP1A2, CYP2C19, and CYP3A4 were identified, and moderate to poor aqueous solubility classifications were recorded across thermodynamic descriptors. Crucially, the authors emphasized that these computational observations are strictly in silico predictions that cannot capture physiological complexity, requiring subsequent in vitro biophysical assays, surface plasmon resonance binding studies, cytotoxicity profiling, and cell-culture validation to confirm therapeutic efficacy against live human metapneumovirus.
